articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO After Affairs: Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO After Affairs: Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Apple CEO Tim Cook, left, speaks with NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang in the Great Hall of the People during a visit to China on May 14, 2026
President Trump suggested on Thursday that Tim Cook, former CEO of Apple, should become the leader of chip maker Nvidia following its chief executive Jensen Huang ’s resignation over his alleged affairs with two women.
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend! ” Trump posted on TruthSocial.
Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday morning, in the wake of reports that he had allegedly been involved in two affairs, including one with a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese spy.
It is unclear if Trump has reached out to Cook regarding this suggestion. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Huang and the White House have maintained a close relationship since the start of Trump’s second term. During his official visit to China in May, Trump invited Huang to attend the summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The New York Times reported that the President insisted on inviting Huang to join the delegation despite concerns over Huang’s relationship with a woman who is believed to be a Chinese spy.
Speaking with reporters on Monday, Trump repeatedly downplayed Huang’s alleged affair, insisting that he believed the tech billionaire’s assertion that he knew nothing about the alleged espionage operation.
“I really believe him,” Trump told reporters during the White House press conference. “I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

articles.title_orig: Ireland faces pressure to stop sending Russia an ingredient vital to its war on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Ireland faces pressure to stop sending Russia an ingredient vital to its war on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
After being moored along Ireland’s boggy River Shannon estuary this week, the 120-metre-long (400-foot-long) cargo ship Karin set sail for Russia.
The vessel was laden with a bulk cargo of white powder that can be forged into weapons which are vital to Moscow’s war on Ukraine .
Alumina, a key ingredient in aluminium, goes into products from toothpaste and lipstick to missiles and drones.
A Russian-owned plant in southern Ireland operates as Europe’s biggest alumina refinery, regularly sending shiploads of the substance directly to St Petersburg and other Russian ports.
Almost five years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, alumina has escaped European sanctions intended to hobble Russia’s economy . That leaves the refinery in Aughinish free to send its product to Russia, where experts say some ends up in weapons.
“The material is clearly ending up in military supplies," said Irish politician Ivana Bacik, who leads the opposition Labour Party.
“It would be unthinkable for Ireland to be contributing, even in that indirect way, to Putin’s war machine.”
Ireland faces mounting calls to halt the shipments as dozens of European leaders gather in Dublin this week to discuss support for Ukraine. A summit of the 47-nation European Political Community on Thursday is being followed by a meeting of European Union leaders.
Irish government minister Niall Collins said that "there’s absolutely no evidence" the material is ending up in military supply chains, though the government has declined to publish the findings of its investigation into the alumina shipments.
Aughinish Alumina said in a statement its product “has no connection to the Russian military supply chain” and that it hired an independent company to provide monthly audits to Irish authorities for “enhanced traceability.”
Alumina is a chemical compound refined from bauxite, a red ore mined primarily in Guinea, Australia and China. The chalky white substance can be smelted into aluminum, which is then forged with other, rarer elements to make strong, heat-resistant and flexible alloys used in missiles and aircraft; aluminum is also used in the manufacture of rocket fuel and explosives.
The Aughinish plant in County Limerick was built in the 1970s and bought in 2007 by Rusal, a Russian aluminum producer. The company was founded, and is still part-owned, by Oleg Deripaska, a sanctioned oligarch with ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Rusal makes virtually all of Russia's aluminum, according to the US and Australian governments.
While many cargo ships leave Aughinish bound for Europe and beyond, a steady stream of them heads straight to the port of St. Petersburg, according to data from MarineTraffic.
The activist group Alumina 22, which is lobbying to sanction the trade in alumina to Russia, estimated that between March and October some 491,307 metric tons of alumina from Ireland was shipped to Russia.
These shipments have grown in importance. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, two alumina factories – one in Australia, the other in Ukraine – stopped exporting to Russia, crimping its supplies by about 40 per cent, according to a 2026 report by the Economic Security Council of Ukraine, or ESCU.
Roughly 17 per cent of Rusal's alumina supply now comes from Ireland, according to ESCU.
An investigation by the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and the Irish Times , published earlier this year, found that alumina from Aughinish is smelted in Russia into aluminum, with some of it sold to a metals trading company that supplies Russian defense contractors.
“Virtually everything that comes from Rusal is with a high probability ending up in the hands of Russian military enterprises,” said Olena Yurchenko, director of analytics, research and investigations at the ESCU.
Standing next to Irish President Micheál Martin in Dublin in June, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said: “Unfortunately, there are companies in Europe that are owned or effectively controlled by Russia and its sanctioned oligarchs. They keep supplying the aggressor with essential materials, even now.”
Mr Martin acknowledged that “we do not want to be in a position where material emanating from a plant in Ireland goes to support the Russian war machine.”
Ireland has not found evidence that is happening — but also no proof it is not, said Enterprise Minister Peter Burke, who is in charge of the country's sanctions enforcement. He said in July it had been impossible to prove Rusal’s assertion that alumina from Ireland is only used to make aluminum for export from Russia.
The Irish government has not published its findings, but it handed them to the European Commission, which drafts EU sanctions packages.
EU sanctions envoy David O’Sullivan said there is little doubt that “the alumina goes to smelters in Russia who produce stuff which undoubtedly goes at least in part to the military-industrial complex”.
“I’ve read the government report. Personally, I think there’s no doubt the investigative journalists got it right,” he said in October in Dublin at a meeting organized by the Institute of International and European Affairs.
The European Parliament in July passed a non-binding motion calling for a ban on alumina exports to Russia. But alumina was not included in the EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia that month. The EU’s executive European Commission, which draws up sanctions packages, is now sounding out member nations about the Irish alumina exports. Sanctions must be agreed upon unanimously by the bloc's 27 countries.
A commission spokesperson said in July that the bloc’s sanctions policy was “a delicate balance” between thwarting Russia’s war effort and limiting “negative impacts” on EU member nations, “especially considering that alumina is a critical raw material”.
Supporters of the plant point to the hundreds of jobs it provides, and to its role as a key source of alumina for European countries. Keeping supply lines open is especially important because of the chokehold on cargo traffic through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Mr Collins, who represents County Limerick in Ireland's parliament, said Ireland has been "hugely resolute in our support for the Ukrainians, and Ukraine hasn’t provided any evidence that Aughinish is doing anything adverse”.
Opposition politicians remain skeptical. Ms Bacik's left-of-center Labour Party supports a temporary nationalisation of the refinery, similar to when Ireland seized banks in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. She says the refinery can ban exports to Russia and find other eager customers in Europe.
“We need to see much stronger action being taken on this from other EU countries if the Irish government isn’t willing to do the right thing here,” she said.
In Foynes, the wind-swept port town beside the plant, many work at Aughinish or know someone who does. But some locals have mixed feelings.
“It's too big a business for them to close it down,” said retired docker Joe Hanlon. “Too much employment for the government to get involved.”
But he said “of course they should”, if Ireland wants “to stop the war on Ukraine”.

articles.title_orig: United Airlines blocks AI agents from booking flights
articles.title_zh: United Airlines blocks AI agents from booking flights
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
An artificial intelligence assistant can help plan your next vacation, but United Airlines wants you to book the flights yourself.
The airline is blocking unauthorized AI agents from using its website, app and other platforms to book or manage flights, it announced Wednesday.
The move aims to protect customers as the airline fears AI assistants could expose personal information, make purchases without customers' knowledge or run into problems with federal aviation rules.
“Protecting our customers’ data and accounts is a priority for United,” the airline said in a news release.
United's app lets travelers handle just about every part of a trip, from booking flights and picking seats to changing reservations when bad weather throws off their plans. But letting an outside AI assistant take over those tasks could create problems, particularly when it has access to a customer's account.
“On the other hand, sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles,” the airline said.
There are also some things United says AI assistants shouldn't handle. For example, passengers must personally confirm during check-in that their checked bags don't contain prohibited items.
“Plus, these automated AI actions have the potential to violate FAA and DOT regulations,” the airline said.
United CEO Scott Kirby has praised AI's potential to solve complex problems during an event in Chicago Tuesday and said the airline will take a cautious approach to AI-powered bookings.
“To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman,” Kirby said, the Wall Street Journal reports .
Airlines have spent years battling third-party booking sites and online travel agencies over how their fares are shown and sold, according to the outlet. AI agents could add another layer to that process, potentially changing how customers find and purchase tickets.
United said it isn't seeing many reservations made through AI agents. Still, its system can also tell where a booking comes from, whether it's made by a traveler, a traditional travel agency or an AI assistant.
The airline reported $2.1 billion in distribution expenses in 2025, making control over how tickets are sold an important part of its business. Booking directly through United's website or app also gives the airline more control over the customer experience.
United isn't the only company taking a closer look at AI agents. Banks, like JPMorgan Chase , and retailers, including Amazon , are also trying to protect customer accounts and information, CNBC reports.
“Corporate leaders in the banking and retail industries have taken similar actions regarding AI agents, and we encourage others to consider measures that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety,” United said.
The airline plans to update its Digital Trust Center with information about the restrictions, tips for protecting accounts and guidance for customers whose AI assistants take unintended actions.
“As personal AI assistants evolve, United will continue to evaluate how these tools interact with our services, with a focus on protecting our customers,” the airline said.

articles.title_orig: IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap: What it means for your money
articles.title_zh: IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap: What it means for your money
articles.content_orig:
The IRS has announced new retirement account contribution limits for 2027.
In its release on Thursday, the agency increased the 401(k) employee deferral limit to $25,500 next year, up from $24,500 in 2026. The change applies to 401(k)s, 403(b)s and most 457 plans, along with the federal Thrift Savings Plan.
The IRS also unveiled 2027 catch-up contribution limits for savers age 50 and older, new individual retirement account savings limits and higher income thresholds for Roth IRA contributions.
Starting in 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution limit will rise to $8,500 for savers 50 and older, up from $8,000 in 2026. But investors aged 60 to 63 can instead save an extra $11,750, based on changes enacted via Secure 2.0 . That figure is up $500 from 2026.
Both amounts are in addition to the $25,500 deferral limit for 2027.
The 2027 IRA contribution limit is $7,500, unchanged from 2026, the IRS announced. IRA catch-up contributions for investors age 50 and older will be $1,100, the same as 2026.
The announcement comes one week after the agency released dozens of other inflation adjustments for 2027, including federal income tax brackets , higher capital gains brackets , estate and gift tax exemptions and provisions impacting families, among others.
In 2025, only 14% of participants maxed out their 401(k)s , according to Vanguard's 2026 How America Saves report, which was based on data from more than 1,300 qualified plans and nearly 5 million participants. The average combined savings rate, including employer deposits, was an estimated 12.1%, according to the same report.
"Before worrying about contribution limits, make sure you're capturing your full employer match," said Sean Michael Pearson, a certified financial planner with Ameriprise Financial Services in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania.
During the second quarter of 2026, about 19% of employees weren't deferring enough to 401(k)s to receive their company's full matching contribution, according to a Fidelity analysis of 27,300 corporate plans and nearly 26 million participants.
Vanguard suggests saving 12% to 15% of your pay per year, including employer contributions, depending on your income. But only one-quarter of 401(k) participants deferred more than 10% of earnings in 2025, according to Vanguard's report.
If you plan to max out your 401(k) for 2027, you should change your savings rate in December so it's active by your first January paycheck, experts say. The update could take one or two pay periods to go into effect.
The "most important habit" is consistently increasing your 401(k) savings rate over time, according to Pearson.
For example, if you bump 401(k) contributions by 1% every year, "you may barely notice the difference in your paycheck, but the long-term impact can be substantial," he said.
In 2025, about 27% of 401(k) plans automatically increased employee deferrals over time, known as "auto-escalation," according to the Plan Sponsor Council of America's yearly survey of 401(k)s . The nonprofit trade organization's survey included 753 plans.
The vast majority of plans with auto-escalation, 69%, boosted deferrals by 1% per year, the Plan Sponsor Council of America found.

articles.title_orig: US envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then head for Dublin to see Zelenskyy
articles.title_zh: US envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then head for Dublin to see Zelenskyy
articles.content_orig:
President Trump’s envoys went to Moscow on Thursday to seek agreement from President Vladimir V. Putin to bring Europe into talks on the war in Ukraine, as the Kremlin pushes to widen the negotiations to overhaul European security arrangements.
The envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, arrived in Russia one day after mediating peace talks in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian representatives, who spoke directly for the first time in nine months. After meeting with Mr. Putin in the Kremlin, the envoys were scheduled to travel to Dublin to meet with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine.
Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner are pressing to involve Europe in the talks as Russia makes clear that it will not consider a cease-fire until its broader demands to redraw the European security architecture are addressed.
The Trump administration, seeking a foreign policy win after Republicans’ drubbing in the midterm elections, is making another push for peace even as Russia gives no indication that it will stop the war anytime soon, and in fact appears to be hardening some of its positions.
Russia has intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities ahead of a winter bombing campaign, taking advantage of Ukraine’s lack of air defenses. On Thursday, Mr. Zelensky said that the Ukrainian armed forces were again facing restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the satellite internet network Starlink, and had asked the United States for information.

articles.title_orig: Trump says Apple’s Tim Cook should take over Nvidia
articles.title_zh: Trump says Apple’s Tim Cook should take over Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., discusses the resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia, the need for an investigations and the national security implications if China gains access to U.S. chips on 'Varney & Co.'
President Donald Trump suggested Thursday that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should replace Jensen Huang as the head of Nvidia following Huang's abrupt resignation amid scrutiny of his personal conduct and potential national security concerns.
"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The president's endorsement comes as Nvidia faces a leadership shake-up following Huang's departure from the artificial intelligence chipmaker he co-founded in 1993.
NVIDIA CEO JENSEN HUANG RESIGNS AMID INVESTIGATION INTO RELATIONSHIP WITH ALLEGED CHINESE SPY
Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., and President Donald Trump. (Graeme Sloan/Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg)
Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO on Thursday while its board searches for a permanent successor, considering candidates from both inside and outside the company.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks during the G20 Innovation Ministerial on Sept. 2, 2026, in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. (Sean Rayford/Getty Images)
Cook stepped down as Apple's CEO in September after 15 years at the helm and now serves as the iPhone maker's executive chairman. Trump did not indicate whether Cook had expressed interest in taking the helm at Nvidia.
Huang's resignation followed reports of two extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.
The allegations raised questions about whether the longtime technology executive could have been targeted by Chinese intelligence, given Nvidia's central role in the global artificial intelligence industry and ongoing U.S.-China tensions over advanced chips.
No evidence has been publicly established that Huang disclosed confidential information or that the woman obtained Nvidia secrets. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto)
The reported relationship has fueled concerns about potential foreign intelligence efforts to gain access to sensitive information involving one of America's most strategically important technology companies. However, no evidence has been publicly established that Huang disclosed confidential information or that the woman obtained Nvidia secrets.

Trump had previously defended Huang, saying Monday that he believed the executive's account that he was unaware of the woman's alleged intelligence ties.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: US FDA shelves commissioner's voucher program for speedy drug reviews, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: US FDA shelves commissioner's voucher program for speedy drug reviews, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The FDA has quietly shelved the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher (CNPV) pilot program, a controversial speedy review process launched by former agency head Marty Makary, M.D., Reuters reports , citing six sources familiar with the matter, as well as internal documents.
Meanwhile, the FDA also appears to have paused publishing complete response letters after briefly halting—and then resuming—the practice in July.
The CNPV was designed to accelerate reviews for drugs and companies that support U.S. national interests, such as meeting large unmet medical needs and onshoring of development and manufacturing. The ultra-accelerated process shortens the FDA’s review from the regular 10 months to just one to two months.
The pilot’s rollout since June 2025 has been controversial, as public concerns run the gamut from political favoritism and lack of transparency to straining the FDA’s bandwidth. So far, 22 drug programs have received the voucher, with 12 approvals and one rejection to date.
The reported pause doesn’t appear to be permanent. In a statement to Fierce, an HHS spokesperson said work under the CNPV is “ongoing.” At least for programs that have already received a CNPV, the FDA is committed to executing on the promised timeline.
“FDA career staff continue to evaluate applications granted a CNPV, meet commitments for accelerated review and enhanced engagement, and assess best practices emerging from the pilot program,” the spokesperson said.
The FDA is still accepting applications for CNPV but is not reviewing or granting new ones, Reuters reported, citing one person familiar with the process. The most recent CNPV grants appear to be for a trio of psychedelics in April following an executive order from President Donald Trump, and one disclosed in May for Partner Therapeutics’ cholangiocarcinoma drug Bizengri. There’s no public record of any new CNPVs following Makary’s resignation as the FDA commissioner in mid-May.
The council of FDA leadership responsible for making critical decisions around CNPV has gone dormant, Reuters asserted, citing internal documents. The FDA’s recent review documents for Revolution Medicines’ pancreatic cancer drug Rasonque, which was among the cohort of nine programs that got the initial batch of CNPVs, do not show any involvement of the council. Instead, the review was conducted and decided by the Oncology Center of Excellence under the pre-existing real-time oncology review framework.
Controversy over the program flared up in May when Sanofi reportedly asked that its diabetes drug Tzield be withdrawn from the CNPV track after then-director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, Tracy Beth Høeg, M.D., Ph.D., tried to overturn staff’s recommendation for approval.
After a leadership overhaul, the FDA in June held a public hearing about CNPV. While existing CNPV beneficiaries voiced support for the program by highlighting a sense of collaboration, they also offered suggestions for improvement, such as clearer feedback from the review council.
The medical and academic communities were more critical. Peter Lurie, M.D., a former FDA employee and current president of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, called for the agency to shut down the pilot due to concerns about “politicization in voucher selection and review, strained agency resources and lack of transparency.”
In a statement to Fierce Thursday, the HHS spokesperson said: “FDA will continue advancing reforms aimed at improving efficiency, accelerating scientific review, strengthening public trust, and delivering measurable results for patients, families, and consumers.”
The legality of the CNPV program has also drawn scrutiny. In a February letter (PDF) to Makary, Rep. Jake Auchincloss, a Democratic congressman from the biotech hub that is Massachusetts, suggested that the agency does not have statutory authority to establish CNPV, and he targeted the political nature of the review council.
“My investigation has revealed an FDA replete with conflicts of interest, illegal maneuvers, and political interference,” Auchincloss wrote in the letter.
CNPV isn’t the only initiative launched by Makary that has faced legal pushbacks. Last summer, touting “radical transparency,” the FDA started publishing all complete response letters in a public database in real-time. However, in a Citizen Petition filed in April, the law firm Covington & Burling argued that the practice could be violating federal laws meant to protect confidential information.
As the FDA has included a legislative proposal in its fiscal year 2027 budget request, asking Congress to grant it clear statutory authority to publicly disclose information related to CRLs, the agency appears to have put new releases on hold.
No new entries have been logged into the FDA’s CRL database for the past three months. The most recent one was a manufacturing-related rejection for ITM Isotopes Technologies’ radiopharmaceutical candidate ITM-11 in early August.
Following the legal challenge and after a three-month hiatus, the FDA had initially confirmed to Fierce in July that it had halted the release of those rejection letters. But then the agency released a new batch of CRLs and told Fierce that it plans to publish more “appropriately redacted” CRLs.
In response to Fierce’s questions about CRL disclosure policy Thursday, an FDA spokesperson said: “Transparency and public confidence are central to the FDA's mission. The FDA remains committed to the proactive release of Complete Response Letters and will continue to publish appropriately redacted CRLs.”

articles.title_orig: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.title_zh: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.content_orig:
An Israeli airstrike on a hospital in southern Gaza overnight killed at least six people, the Health Ministry in the Palestinian enclave said Thursday.
The strike hit a surgery building at Nasser Hospital, with medical staff and patients among those killed, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy, health officials said. The Israeli military said it was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants.
The strike — the latest despite an ongoing U.S.-backed ceasefire — shattered ceilings and left debris strewn across wards inside the hospital, which is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza after the destruction of Israel’s yearslong military assault.
Palestinian surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira was among those killed, the Health Ministry said. He was featured in the 2026 documentary “American Doctor,” which followed three American doctors helping to provide medical care in Gaza.
Dr. Ayman Abu Obeid, head of the surgery department at Nasser Hospital, said there was no “notice, warning or anything” before the hospital was attacked. “Suddenly, there was fire and shelling and walls were brought down instantly,” he said.
He said he was not aware of any “resistance fighters or combatants present — only a medical team treating patients.”
NBC News also spoke with two surgeons who said they were in the hospital when the missile struck after traveling to Gaza from the U.K. earlier this month to assist with medical care.
Both Dr. Goher Rahbour, a consultant general and colorectal surgeon, and Dr. Stephan Verborg, a limb reconstruction surgeon, said they were also not aware of any warning from the Israeli military before the strike, which hit the hospital shortly after midnight.
“I heard the impact and I felt the explosion because the whole hospital shook,” Verborg said in a phone interview Thursday. He said he was about 15 to 20 meters away from the point of impact, adding: “You could smell the smoke. You could see the dust.”
Rahbour said he had been operating with Abu Shaira, whom he described as a “lovely” and “affable” person, earlier that day. He said they had been laughing and joking together Wednesday evening in the hours just before the Palestinian surgeon was killed.
Both doctors had traveled to Gaza early this month through the organization IDEALS, a U.K. charity seeking to provide sustainable humanitarian aid to regions affected by conflict or natural disasters. They said they had not seen any indication of a Hamas presence in the hospital.
Tributes were paid to Abu Shaira. “Dr. Rizq was at the hospital during the entire war,” Dr. Mohammed Zaqout, director general of the Health Ministry in Gaza, could be seen telling a crowd of mourners, surrounding a body covered in a shroud, in a video captured for NBC News on Thursday. “He didn’t abandon his duties for even one day.”
Nasser Hospital said a 13-year-old boy, identified as Jihad Naeem Muhammad Abu Tilikh, was also among those killed.
The Israeli military and the Israel Security Agency said they struck a senior Hamas member, along with other militants, who they said had “advanced” attacks from the hospital in the southern Gaza Strip overnight. In a later statement, they identified the senior member as Muhammad Abu Ismail, who they said served as the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade and had also been responsible for holding hostages in Gaza.
The IDF and ISA said Hamas had “established a presence within the hospital complex and used it as a command center” and stored weapons and conducted interrogations and torture from within the medical complex. They shared photos of weapons alleged to have been found within the complex.
The IDF and ISA said steps had been taken to “mitigate harm to civilians, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance.” They also later said “advance warnings were issued to the population.” The IDF said it was looking into reports that medical workers,  including Abu Shaira, and patients were killed.
One woman, Tahani Ibrahim Abu Anza, said her brother, Khaled Abu Anza, was killed in the strike, with Nasser Hospital separately confirming his death.
A number of media outlets, including Israeli media outlet Ynet , reported that a commander in Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade of that same name was killed in the strike. Asked to confirm that and whether he was directly targeted, the IDF said it would get back on the matter.
Tahani Ibrahim Abu Anza did not directly identify her brother, 53, as a Hamas member, but said she believed he was targeted. He had been at the hospital for physical therapy after undergoing surgery, she said.
“He did not come to the hospital to engage in combat or resistance. He came for medical treatment,” she said.
Hamas condemned the allegations that it was using the hospital for military operations as “lies of the criminal enemy” and called the attack a “war crime.”
Hospitals have protected status under international law, but they have been heavily targeted under Israel’s yearslong offensive in Gaza. The Israeli military has repeatedly accused Hamas of operating within medical facilities, a charge the militant group has denied.
The overnight attack was not the first time that Nasser Hospital itself has been targeted.
In August 2025, the hospital was hit by a double tap Israeli strik e that killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers. The deadly attack sparked international outrage.
Of Gaza’s 37 hospitals, just two are considered to be “fully functioning,” while 18 are partially functioning and 17 are considered nonfunctioning after much of the enclave’s healthcare system was devastated under Israel’s offensive, according to data published by the World Health Organization.
Israeli strikes have continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreement reached in October of last year.
More than 1,600 people have been killed since the truce came into effect, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry in the enclave. Israel says four of its ⁠soldiers have ​been killed in that time.
Both Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire.
More than 74,600 people, including thousands of children, have been killed overall in Gaza since Israel launched its offensive in the enclave following the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, in which some 1,200 people were killed and around 250 taken hostage.
In a statement, Medical Aid for Palestinians, which supports several departments at Nasser Hospital, said the overnight attack was “yet another indication that the so-called ‘ceasefire’ has brought neither safety nor an end to Israel’s attacks on Gaza’s healthcare system.”
The latest strikes come as Palestinians contend with heavy rains and desperate conditions in the enclave as the colder months set in, prompting a fresh wave of outcry over the lack of progress in advancing the peace deal between Israel and Hamas.
Chantal Da Silva reports on world news for NBC News Digital and is based in London.

articles.title_orig: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress Has Tried to Tame Nvidia’s Riskiest Bets
articles.title_zh: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress Has Tried to Tame Nvidia’s Riskiest Bets
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia is now facing a scenario few would have considered until very recently - a future without Jensen Huang.
The influential co-founder of the AI chip-making giant resigned on Thursday over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Chief financial officer Colette Kress is in charge, for now, as the tech giant faces one of its biggest challenges - finding the right person to permanently lead the business that Huang helped create more than three decades ago and turned into one of the world's most valuable companies.
We take a look at which candidates have emerged as potential successors.
Colette Kress has been an industry veteran for more than 30 years, having previously held high positions at tech firms like Cisco and Microsoft.
Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's executive vice-president, has seen the firm's transformation from making chips for video games in the early 1990s to becoming an AI semiconductor powerhouse.
She has "fronted every earnings call" alongside Huang and is a "familiar and trusted voice for the market at a time when it badly needs one," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at investment firm eToro.
But doing the job permanently could be a different story, said Gilbert, as the firm, known for its edge in technology, could want an engineer in the chair.
Another option is Chris Malachowsky, who founded Nvidia alongside Huang and Curtis Priem, and is the only executive that shares the same level of seniority.
Malachowsky has played a key part in developing the company's computing technology.
Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's high-performance computing business, has also emerged as a potential candidate if the company is keen to put an engineer in the top job.
Buck was among the early pioneers who helped popularise the use of graphic processors beyond gaming applications.
"He could protect Nvidia's technological edge, but his ability to manage the wider commercial relationships and geopolitical challenges would face scrutiny," said Charu Chanana, investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.
Today, Nvidia's leading processors are widely regarded as the gold standard for AI development.
Huang's children also work at Nvidia in executive positions but are relatively young and inexperienced.
Nvidia is likely to favour an internal appointment initially but could look externally for a more permanent replacement, said Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap.
Several names of tech entrepreneurs outside of Nvidia have been floated by experts.
Liu said Apple's former chief executive, Tim Cook, could be a possible choice as someone familiar with managing global supply chains, though she questioned whether he would be willing to leave the iPhone maker, where he is the chair.
Liu and Chanana also suggested Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm Holdings, the UK chipmaking giant.
Nvidia's processors are made with the help of chipmakers around the world, including Taiwan's TSMC and South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung.
Haas is familiar with leading a publicly-listed company and would bring semiconductor experience, though Nvidia's business model is considerably different from Arm's, said Chanana.
"The challenge is finding someone who can combine Jensen's technical understanding, strategic vision and relationships across the global technology industry," Liu said.
Ten Cap's Liu had believed it was just a matter of time before Huang would step down as Nvidia's chief executive.
"The issue is no longer simply about personal conduct," she said. "It is about corporate governance, national security concerns and maintaining confidence in the leadership of one of the world's most strategically important companies."
Several major investment firms have downgraded their forecasts for the chip giant - a rare shift given investors' longstanding optimism about the company.
An early indication came as markets opened in New York shortly after Huang's resignation was announced.
Nvidia shares opened down more than 13%, wiping more than half a trillion dollars off the firm's share market value.
Stacy Rasgon, senior analyst in US semiconductors at Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors that "our gut tells us we probably haven't fully probed the depths of what might be found here".
Rasgon halved Bernstein's share price target for Nvidia and said: "We've had enough and prefer to watch from the sidelines."
Ray Wang, chief executive of Constellation Research, said the crisis isn't so much an issue for the wider AI industry but rather one for Nvidia itself which has to consider if the person it appoints as its chief executive has the same appeal as Huang.
"That's really what the issue is, because a lot of these partnerships and investments have been made because of the trust with with Jensen," he said.
Additional reporting by Kali Hays

articles.title_orig: Stocks Slide on Nvidia Troubles, Oil Edges Lower: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks Slide on Nvidia Troubles, Oil Edges Lower: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s shares plummeted Thursday, sending tremors through global markets, as the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang , stepped down from his role.
Shares in Nvidia dropped as much as 14 percent when markets opened for trading on Thursday, extending a decline that has wiped out more than $1 trillion from the company’s market value this month alone. The stock began to reverse most of its losses by late morning.
The broader market rose slightly, too, as investors began to conclude that the fallout of Mr. Jensen’s departure would not fundamentally undermine the artificial intelligence trade. Yields on the 10-year U.S. Treasury rose above 5 percent on Thursday for the first time in weeks. Yields go up when Treasury prices go down.
Nvidia has emerged as central to the A.I. economy because its chips — or graphic processing units — help train and power models across the industry. It has also become a central bank of sorts for several A.I. companies, because its finances are deeply intertwined with those of everyone from frontier A.I. labs to neoclouds, which rent out computing power.
“This is an Nvidia problem before it is an A.I. problem,” said Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial. But he added that Nvidia’s woes could trickle through to other companies.
“Where I would be careful is with the smaller A.I. cloud companies that leaned on Nvidia’s checkbook,” he said. “If the new regime gets more conservative about financing its own customers, that is where it shows up first.”

SpaceX is counting down to make history with the launch of its Starship Flight 15 mission on Friday, Nov. 13 , with liftoff scheduled for 5:45 p.m. EDT (2245 GMT) at Starbase, Texas. Starship Flight 15 will attempt to land both Starship Ship and Super Heavy Booster. It will be the first-ever full recovery of an orbital rocket and spacecraft, if successful.
Follow our Starship Flight 15 coverage here as SpaceX completes its final prelaunch work for the launch, which will also deliver 26 new Starlink V3 satellites into orbit.

STARBASE, Texas — We are one day until launch of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15, and Space.com is onsite here in Texas prepping cameras and coverage.
Liftoff is currently targeted for tomorrow (Nov. 13), during a 75-minute window opening at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT).
This flight could be a historic one for SpaceX and the space industry. For the first time, SpaceX will attempt to catch both stages of its massive Starship rocket — Super Heavy just minutes after launch, and the Ship upper stage roughly 22 hours later, following several orbits around Earth.
I'll be covering the action from here in Texas, so stay tuned to Space.com for updates as we count down to liftoff!
Happy Wednesday, Space Fans. We are now T-2 days away from SpaceX's planned launch of its Starship Flight 15 test mission, so I wanted to take a moment to give you a run down on what to expect.
Today, you can read my full guide to SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch here , which goes over what time and where to watch the launch online. Liftoff is on track for Friday, Nov. 13, at 4:45 p.m. CST, which is 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT). But it ALSO (and this is new) includes what time to tune in a day later for the planned Starship upper stage (Ship) landing and catch by the metal "Chopstick" arms of its landing pad at SpaceX's Starbase facility in South Teas.
If you're wondering how the rocket's assembly is going, our Spaceflight Editor Mike Wall has this update on the Starship Flight 15 Super Heavy booster going through final catch tests yesterday. Flight 15 will mark the first time SpaceX will attempt to land and catch both the Super Heavy booster (which it has done several times) and the Ship from orbit.
If successful, it will be the first full recovery of an entire orbital rocket from space.
Hello, Space Fans, and welcome to our coverage of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight , the first ever to attempt twin landings of the Starship Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage.
SpaceX has officially set the launch date for Flight 15 for Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EDT (2145 GMT) . That puts launch just about 3 days away and Space.com will provide live coverage of the potentially historic flight, the first full recovery of an orbital rocket.
Space.com Spaceflight Writer Josh Dinner will be reporting live from near SpaceX's Starbase , Texas site for the launch, with myself (Tariq Malik), Spaceflight and Tech Editor Mike Wall and other team members tracking the flight remotely for you here. articles.title_orig: How Hamas shaped Gaza's winter flooding narrative before the first storm
articles.title_zh: How Hamas shaped Gaza's winter flooding narrative before the first storm
articles.content_orig:
“There was flooding in Gaza , but the narrative and scale of suffering was written by Hamas before it even started raining,” Justin Pozmanter, News Director at HonestReporting, told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.
Pozmanter shared an exclusive report with the Post detailing how the Hamas-government winter campaign and a Hamas-run media office figure traveled from Telegram to the international press between November 1 and 10, 2026.
The story begins on November 1, when the Gaza Winter Emergency Committee, a Hamas-government body, issued its first press statement, posted on the GMO’s Telegram channel.
The committee announced the “2026-2027 Winter Preparedness and Response Plan” and the national campaign “Together Towards a Safe Winter.” The release predicted a harsh, early winter and blamed Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery, spare parts, fuel, and shelter supplies.
It also provided a list of figures: 200,000 worn-out tents and one million tarps needed; 7,800 tents in dangerous locations; 2,000 cracked buildings at risk of collapse; and 70% of municipalities’ basic operating equipment destroyed.
Days later, on November 5, before any storm in the region, Euro-Med Monitor published an article named “Israel weaponises cold weather against Palestinians in Gaza for fourth year, continues to ban shelter supplies.”
Many of the article’s claims can be traced directly back to the November 1 Hamas press release. For example, the article writes “Israel continues to deprive Palestinians in the Gaza Strip of safe shelter for the fourth consecutive year.” It then lists the same figures that appeared in the Hamas memo: 200,000 tents; one million tarps; 2,000 cracked buildings.
As HonestReporting noted, this was a pivot point.
The Hamas-aligned framing, such as “Israel is engineering a winter catastrophe,” was restated in the vocabulary of a human rights NGO, with figures sourced to a committee whose Hamas governance ties go unlabeled.
The first winter storm arrived on November 6, with footage of floods in Gaza circulating on social media.
A day later, on November 7 at 11:15 Israel time, roughly 12 hours after the first rain, the Hamas-run Government Media Office published a new press statement warning that “Within 12 hours: 70,000 tents flooded and $3 million in losses.”
It claimed dozens of walls collapsed, causing injuries, and warned that cracked buildings damaged in the “genocide war” may collapse, and holds Israel “fully responsible” for keeping crossings closed to shelter and reconstruction material. It also called on the international community and UN bodies to intervene.
Within a few hours, Reuters , the BBC, and NBC News began posting the “70,000 tents” figure. Reuters was the only one of the three that explicitly identified the GMO as Hamas-run.
Hamas-linked Gaza flooding claims gain traction on social media
However, by November 8, the figures stopped being attributed to the Gazan ministries or Hamas. Drop Site News, for example, credits the “950,000 at risk of flooding” figure to “the UN.”
Anti-Israel social media accounts then began amplifying the claims.
Drop Site News called it “deliberate and systematic cruelty... part of an effort to drive Palestinians out of Gaza... with full US support.”
Pro-Palestinian British doctor Rahmeh Aladwan said: “The Jewish occupation destroyed 82% of Gaza and has blocked caravans and building material for 3 years.”
Greta Thunberg posted on Facebook: “around 70,000 tents flooded... ISRAEL IS FULLY RESPONSIBLE. END THE GENOCIDE.”
HonestReporting also noted that the Hamas-run Gaza Government Media Office announced the 70,000 tents figure just hours after the rain began, and already estimated losses to be roughly three million dollars.
HonestReporting questioned how Hamas, in a matter of hours and during a downpour, definitively knew that 70,000 tents had been flooded.
In other countries, after a disaster strikes, it can take up to a few days for officials to even attain a preliminary estimate of the scope of the damage.
Few news sites mentioned the extensive preparations Israel went to make the Strip ready for bad weather.
Since September 4, 2026, roughly two months before the recent storm, COGAT (the Israeli Ministry of Defense body responsible for humanitarian coordination in Palestinian areas) has been posting on social media the steps it was taking in anticipation of the upcoming winter in the Gaza Strip.
This has included facilitating the entry of tents and shelter equipment, engine oil, generators and lights, medical equipment and supplies, tarpaulins, winter clothing, vacuum trucks, portable toilets, and spare vehicle parts.
By the time the storm arrived this past weekend, COGAT said that over 91,000 tents and 8,200 trucks full of winter necessities had entered the Gaza Strip since the beginning of the winterization campaign in September.
“COGAT will continue working in cooperation with the Board of Peace, the UN, international organizations, and the international community to maintain the humanitarian situation in the Gaza Strip at its current stable level ahead of the winter, while taking the necessary measures to prevent Hamas from seizing control of the humanitarian aid and essential supplies,” COGAT wrote on November 5.
As Pozmanter said, there was indeed flooding in Gaza, but the narrative and scale of suffering were written by Hamas before it even started raining.
“In their telling, parroted by affiliated organizations like Euro-med and largely trusted as fact by the press and many Western leaders, Israel was to blame, despite facilitating distribution of tens of thousands of tents and tons of winter gear to the population, something no other country has ever done for an enemy population during war,” he told the Post .
He also noted that, largely absent from the coverage, were any mentions that Hamas has “dismantled Israeli and donor-provided sewage and drainage systems and used the pipes to build rockets, and spent billions in international aid to build a vast tunnel network for themselves rather than infrastructure for their people.”
“The truth is, Hamas once again sacrificed Gazan civilians and the media, once again, demonstrated that it waives scrutiny when unverified accusations are leveled at Israel,” Pozmanter concluded.

articles.title_orig: European leaders reject Russian push to overhaul continent’s security
articles.title_zh: European leaders reject Russian push to overhaul continent’s security
articles.content_orig:
Joe is based in Brussels, where he focuses on European politics and defence. He has covered the Ukraine war and its peace negotiations and reported on US elections from Washington DC
Britain and France should immediately deploy troops to Ukraine, a former head of Nato has said.
Anders Fogh Rasmussen accused Europe’s two nuclear powers of presiding over a “coalition of the waiting” while the Kremlin dragged out peace talks.
“For some months, France and the UK have tried to establish a coalition of the willing, but it’s more now a coalition of the waiting,” the 73-year-old former Danish prime minister told The Telegraph from his office in Brussels.
“We should transform that into a ‘coalition of the doing’ by deploying troops… you could not wait for a peace deal but actually push for peace by telling Putin ‘you cannot deter us, and we will help the Ukrainians defend against attacks against their critical infrastructure’.”
Mr Rasmussen’s call for action came during US-led negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine and Russia, which focused on security guarantees and preventing a future war.
European officials were kept out of the room after Moscow objected to their involvement in the two-day talks, which Ukraine described on Wednesday as “one of the toughest” negotiations yet.
Vladimir Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, said after the talks: “We have no idea what the Europeans are doing here, this is a trilateral meeting. They can hang out in the lobby if they want.”
Mr Rasmussen, who was Nato’s secretary-general between 2009 and 2014, believes that Europe must show Vladimir Putin that it is serious in its support for Ukraine, even as it continues to be denied a seat at the table.
He has devised a five-point strategy to stop the war and prevent Europe from “sleepwalking into a permanent war on the Continent”.
He called on Germany, Spain and Greece to empty their stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to help Kyiv protect itself against Russian ballistic missile attacks, and suggested Nato extends its integrated air and missile defence systems over western Ukraine to bolster defences.
On top of this, Mr Rasmussen said the EU should confiscate more than €200bn (£175bn) in frozen Russian assets and use them to top up Kyiv’s defence budget. The “Coalition of the Willing” should be overhauled to include only countries willing to go to war with Russia should it attack Ukraine after any ceasefire is negotiated, he added.
“President Trump has chosen Moscow and sided with Vladimir Putin,” Mr Rasmussen said. “So in Europe, we have a particular responsibility for helping Ukraine, and that’s why I call on European leaders to wake up.”
He added: “It’s clear that the Russians do not want peace. Putin has no incentives to engage in the peace negotiations as long as he believes he can succeed on the battlefield.
“So, we need to change his calculus, we need to put more pressure on Russia.”
His plan would involve French and British troops as a “reassurance force” to protect Ukraine’s population centres.
It would also free up more Ukrainian resources to commit to the front line with Russia.
Mr Rasmussen insisted that such a deployment would be in line with international rules as long as it was requested by Kyiv.
However, Mr Rasmussen’s ideas are likely to be controversial amongst Europe’s Nato allies.
Numerous countries have said they would not actively shoot down Russian missiles over Ukrainian territory for fear of becoming a genuine party to the conflict.
Belgium has repeatedly blocked EU discussions about using a tranche of frozen Russian assets to fund Ukraine’s defence.
While Germany has recently warned that it cannot donate any more Patriot interceptor missiles because it doesn’t have the stockpiles to defend its own country.
“Maybe Poland is in a different situation, but Germany, I don’t understand why they cannot deliver those Patriot systems. Deliver them now; they are needed right now in Ukraine… Germany is not threatened now,” Mr Rasmussen said.
The former Nato chief, who was involved in talks with Russia when it first invaded Ukraine’s Crimea peninsula in 2014, said the Continent was right to reopen communication channels with Moscow.
But he warned against linking discussions on a ceasefire in Ukraine to negotiations over a future European security architecture, arguing that Putin would seek to exploit the talks to restrict the military capabilities of both Kyiv and the alliance.
That said, Mr Rasmussen believes Nato could ultimately offer Russia security guarantees, given that its allies have no plans to attack Moscow.
“Why not? It wouldn’t cost anything to give such a security guarantee,” he concluded.

The Israeli military struck a hospital in the southern Gaza Strip on Thursday, killing at least six people and injuring 28 more, according to local health officials.
Dr. Ahmed al-Farra, general director of Nasser Hospital, said in a news conference on Thursday that two missiles had hit the facility and that among the dead was Rezeq Abu Shaira, 52, a doctor.
Health officials reached in Gaza by phone said that a man called Khaled Abu Anza had also been killed. A spokeswoman for the Israeli military, speaking on condition of anonymity in line with protocol, said that Mr. Abu Anza was a Hamas operative.
The Israeli security agency and military said in a joint statement on Thursday that they had targeted Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom they identified as a Hamas commander “responsible for holding numerous hostages captive” during the Gaza war.
The Israeli authorities said that Hamas had established a command center at the hospital complex to stage operations against Israeli forces and was storing weapons there. They added that steps had been taken to mitigate harm to civilians.
Hamas said the Israeli claim that the hospital was used for military activity was a “blatant attempt to justify a heinous crime targeting a civilian medical facility.” Residents of Gaza have said that officials affiliated with Hamas-run Gaza government and security forces sometimes use the enclave’s hospitals as offices.

articles.title_orig: Senator opens investigation into evidence RFK Jr ‘unlawfully lied’ to Congress
articles.title_zh: Senator opens investigation into evidence RFK Jr ‘unlawfully lied’ to Congress
articles.content_orig:
Exclusive: Ron Wyden, citing Guardian report, is launching inquiry into whether health secretary lied about Samoa trip during confirmation hearings
A top Democratic senator has launched an investigation into evidence that Robert F Kennedy Jr “unlawfully lied” in his 2025 confirmation hearings to become the US health secretary, citing a report by the Guardian .
Ron Wyden of Oregon, the incoming chair of the powerful Senate finance committee, is seeking extensive records from Children’s Health Defense (CHD), the non-profit anti-vaccine group Kennedy has used as a vehicle to fuel his political rise, including all documents related to a 2019 trip Kennedy took to Samoa.
“We are beginning an investigation into evidence that Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F Kennedy, Jr unlawfully lied to Congress on multiple occasions,” Wyden said in a letter to the group that was sent on Wednesday and obtained by the Guardian. The letter was also signed by Angela Alsobrooks, a Democratic senator from Maryland.
In the letter, the two lawmakers cited reporting by the Guardian that indicated Kennedy lied about his reasons for going to Samoa in 2019, a trip that occurred just months before a measles outbreak killed 83 people in the Pacific island nation, mostly children under age five.
The trip, which Kennedy made as the chair and chief legal counsel of CHD, became one of the most criticized events in his career before he entered government. Critics, including Samoan officials, have said Kennedy’s presence emboldened anti-vaccine activists in Samoa, worsening a vaccination crisis. Kennedy has denied the allegations, saying he never gave any public statement about vaccines or discouraged Samoans from getting vaccinated.
“We are deeply concerned by the tactics Kennedy has used – both before and during his tenure as secretary – to stand in the way of children receiving life-saving vaccinations,” the two Democratic senators wrote. “In Samoa and in the United States, unvaccinated children have died tragic and preventable deaths during measles outbreaks. We intend to hold Secretary Kennedy accountable for the grave harm he has caused to vulnerable children. We also intend to hold him accountable for any false statements made to Congress, a crime that undermines the Senate’s ability to fulfill its constitutional duties.”
In two congressional confirmation hearings in January 2025, Kennedy told lawmakers who held the key to his confirmation that his visit to Samoa had “nothing to do with vaccines”.
But letters obtained by the Guardian and the Associated Press through an open records lawsuit brought by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press contradicted that testimony. In one he wrote to the Samoan prime minister in January 2019 before the trip, Kennedy explicitly said he wanted to study the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the Pacific island nation. In it, he used the words “vaccine” or “vaccination” eight times.
The prime minister responded a month later , saying Samoa could benefit from CHD’s assessment of MMR vaccines and inviting him to come.
Children’s Health Defense did not respond to requests for comment, and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) did not immediately comment.
HHS previously said in response to the Guardian’s reporting on Kennedy’s Senate testimony that his visit to Samoa was “unrelated to vaccines. Any claim or insinuation based on these letters that Secretary Kennedy lied under oath or to Congress is not only false but outright defamatory.” It has not provided a response to questions about why his testimony contradicted what he said in his letter to the Samoan prime minister.
By requesting documents from CHD, Wyden is aiming at the heart of Kennedy’s political machine. Since taking office, Kennedy has hired former CHD employees, including Lyn Redwood, a former CHD president who made early outreach on his behalf to Samoa . Redwood is now an employee at the HHS, reportedly working on vaccine safety . Kennedy’s closest adviser at HHS, Stefanie Spear, ran CHD’s newsletter before joining his 2024 presidential campaign.
With Kennedy now in government, CHD and its leaders often act as his most vociferous defenders, praising his work and explaining his decisions on their video podcasts, articles and on social media. Kennedy headlined CHD’s annual conference in September, where he made false and misleading claims about the safety of vaccines .
The Senate letter requested all documents related to any travel to Samoa by Kennedy or other employees or associates of CHD and any communications with Samoan government officials. It also asked for records related to Kennedy’s presidential campaign and his Senate confirmation process.
In addition, the senators requested records related to Kennedy’s speech to CHD’s September convention and all communications between CHD and federal government officials since 20 January 2025.
CHD has a deadline of 4 December.
On the night of the election, after polls closed and it became clear Democrats would take a majority of seats in the Senate, Wyden made a social media post with a direct message about accountability. “ Subpoenas ,” he wrote, in the one-word post. Alsobrooks, a member of the Senate committee on health, education, labor and pensions, has repeatedly called on Kennedy to resign or be fired .
The letter does not go as far as the legal force of a subpoena. But it would be a good idea to treat such a letter seriously, said Tim Stretton , of the Project on Government Oversight, a nonpartisan watchdog group in Washington.
“It’s not wise to ignore it,” Stretton said. “It’s really in their interest now to cooperate in a good faith effort.”
If they don’t, he said, the committee or chair could issue subpoenas to demand the information they are seeking.
Knowingly giving material false testimony to Congress is a crime that carries a possible prison sentence, though it is rarely prosecuted.
Wyden previously called for a criminal investigation of Kennedy’s testimony about his trip to Samoa. He said in August he would be pressing Republican colleagues to issue a criminal referral of Kennedy to the Department of Justice for a criminal investigation. He said then that “when Democrats retake the majority in the Senate, RFK will be at the top of the list of Trump officials the finance committee will hold accountable for endangering American families”.
Several other Democrats have called for Kennedy to resign or be impeached. Bernie Sanders, incoming chair of the Senate committee on health, education, labor and pensions, said he is open to impeachment . And the incoming senator Annie Andrews, a pediatrician from South Carolina, has been calling for Kennedy’s impeachment since her campaign.
Legal experts have said it is unlikely the justice department under Trump would prosecute, but said Kennedy’s statements could be used as grounds for hearings, for an impeachment inquiry or to create other obstacles for the Trump administration .

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave and These Other Stocks Are in the Nvidia Danger Zone
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave and These Other Stocks Are in the Nvidia Danger Zone
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite teetered around the flatline on Thursday as investors shrugged off the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and bet it would not derail the whole AI trade.
The Nasdaq Composite was last down 0.1%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 187 points, or 0.4%. The S&P 500 traded up 0.1%.
Selling pressure on Nvidia eased a bit with the stock last down 5%. The shares were down double digits at one point after the company announced that Huang had resigned and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. This comes after Huang reportedly had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Investors moved into competitors of Nvidia, including Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom , helping to bolster the market. AMD shares were up 4%, while Broadcom gained 5%.
Hyperscalers Microsoft and Alphabet — key buyers of Nvidia chips and leaders of the AI rally — also increased.
"This is a golden opportunity for Amazon, for Google, for AMD, for Broadcom, for OpenAI and Anthropic, who are hiring chip experts to help them design their own chips," said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management.
"Nvidia's fate as one company is one thing, but this AI revolution is way bigger than that," he also said. "If Nvidia falls from grace and their chips are no longer the best, and AMDs are better or Google's are better, then people will switch over and buy them. The demand for the chips is not is not going down."
There was a sense from investors that perhaps Huang's exit was a capitulation event for the AI trade with Nvidia's stock down by more than 25% the past one month as this scandal was unfolding.
"We are sticking with the thesis that technology stocks bottomed last week," said Tom Lee, the head of research at Fundstrat, in a note Thursday. Huang's departure "does not change our view."
Stocks outside of technology such as JPMorgan and Eli Lilly traded higher as well.
Oil prices retreated from their highs of the day, also helping sentiment. They initially popped Thursday morning after President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post , "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed."
Paul Meeks says he's buying Nvidia shares with "both hands" despite CEO Jensen Huang's resignation , because the decline amid this unfolding scandal has brought the stock down to "stupid" valuation levels.
The Freedom Capital head of technology research noted that the stock is trading at just 10 times fiscal 2028 earnings estimates after Thursday's decline.
Nvidia shares are off 20% in November alone, pressured by the scandal unfolding.
"I think that the actual announcement of his resignation is a market-clearing event," said Meeks.
CNBC Pro subscribers can learn more about Meeks' other key points here .
Even as Nvidia shares remained lower following CEO Jensen Huang's resignation , the broader market rose as investors moved past the announcement.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite , both of which began Thursday's session lower, rose 0.2% and 0.1%, respectively.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average outperformed, rising 138 points, or 0.3%.
Sales of existing homes fell to their lowest level in more than 16 years during October, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday.
A decline of 5.5% brought the seasonally adjusted annualized rate down to 3.75 million during a month that saw mortgage rates continue to climb, putting pressure on an already beleaguered housing market. The total was the lowest since August 2010.
"Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023," said NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun. "Based on the current underwhelming home sales pace at a time of consistent job growth, there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline."
Nvidia shares are seeing huge volume as the stock drops following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang .
The chipmaker saw more than 373 million shares traded amid the selling pressure. That's above the stock's 30-day average of 144.4 million.
The stock was last down more than 5%.
Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said Thursday she doesn't see the need for aggressive interest rate increases ahead.
While Hammack still supports rate hikes as the Fed struggles to get inflation back to its 2% target, she advocated for a gradual approach that the economy can adapt to more easily.
"I think we need to move rates higher to get to a restrictive stance of policy to bring inflation back down to 2%. My view is that if we go steadily in smaller increments, more frequent, smaller rises, it's easier for businesses and households to manage around that," she sad. "It's less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements."
Earlier in the week, Fed Governor Christopher Waller raised the specter of a half-point hike at the December meeting if the inflation data comes in worse than anticipated. However, Hammack said she doesn't think that's necessary, at least for now.
"If we get behind the curve, and I don't think we're behind the curve today, but if we get behind the curve, then that might be something that we need to consider," she said. "So I'll certainly have an open mind walking into that December meeting."
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite began Thursday's session in the red.
The broad market index fell 0.8% shortly after the opening bell, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq declined 1.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 108 points, or 0.2%.
Shares of Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices gained about 3% each in premarket trading after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia.
The company's chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim chief.
Nvidia shares were last down about 10%.
For more, follow along with our live updates of Nvidia and Jensen Huang here .
Initial jobless claims showed a modest pop last week after hovering around their lowest levels since the late 1960s.
First-time filings for unemployment benefits totaled a seasonally adjusted 200,000 for the week ending Nov. 7, a gain of 9,000 from the prior period and higher than the Dow Jones consensus for 195,000, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
Continuing claims, which run a week behind, fell 20,000 to just below 1.7 million.
Nebius shares plummeted in the premarket on Thursday after the neocloud's third-quarter revenue topped analysts' expectations, but its guidance disappointed investors.
The stock was last down almost 16%. That's after it rose more than 15% in Wednesday's regular session.
— Jordan Novet and Sean Conlon
Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang's future as head of one of the most important names in technology hangs in the balance following revelations that he had an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.
Analysts said his ouster could lead to a 20%-plus decline in the shares with the uncertainty that would follow overhanging the stock a bit longer after that.
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
"Jensen Huang is toast," Bill Blain, founder and principal at Wind Shift Capital, said in his morning newsletter. "Nvidia's dependence on Jensen Huang is now exposed as a major market risk. The dominant firm within the AI industry lacks clear succession planning and Huang was seen as the acceptable face of AI by the public."
U.S. Treasury yields were mixed Thursday as bond trading resumed after the Veterans Day closure and investors looked ahead to fresh inflation and housing data for clues about the economy and the Federal Reserve's next move.
The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note — the benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — were flat at 4.9920%.
The 2-year Treasury note yield, which is more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was 3 basis points higher at 4.7568%. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury note yield — which often moves on geopolitical developments — was steady at 5.3403%.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) was upgraded by William Blair on Thursday, with the brokerage citing an improving risk/reward outlook as its biggest AI chip rival, Nvidia (NVDA), faces leadership uncertainty.

According to a note cited by TheFly, William Blair upgraded AMD to 'Outperform' from 'Market Perform,' saying the stock has room to rise as Nvidia faces scrutiny and a leadership vacuum, while AMD's competitive position improves and its valuation looks attractive.
At the time of writing in premarket trading, AMD stock was up 3% while NVDA stock was down nearly 7%.
William Blair said all four factors behind its previous rating have shifted in AMD's favor since it initiated coverage in July.
Intel's (INTC) Xeon server processor roadmap continues to face delays and supply shortages, while the transition toward Arm-based host processors has proved less disruptive than previously anticipated, Investing.com reported, citing the note.
The firm also noted that AMD's valuation multiple has declined significantly even as earnings estimates have risen.
Analysts at William Blair expect AMD's data-center AI revenue to surpass its server central processing unit (CPU) business in the fourth quarter, supported by its Helios AI systems ramping through 2027. It sees the potential for more than 80% revenue growth next year, over twice its longer-term model.
AMD and Broadcom (AVGO) gained as investors considered whether Nvidia customers might diversify their chip suppliers. Floodlines Research founder Anna Wu told Bloomberg, "AMD as a direct competitor, and Alphabet and Broadcom in the TPU space, are natural beneficiaries in the short term."
Meanwhile, a Barron's report cited Pepperstone analyst Chris Weston, who said markets appeared to distinguish between Nvidia-specific risks and the broader AI trade, suggesting investors were not treating Huang's situation as a fundamental threat to AI demand.
BofA raised its AMD price target to $700 from $650, maintaining a 'Buy' rating, according to TheFly. The firm reiterated AMD as its top central processing unit (CPU) pick, citing its broad product portfolio, leadership across key segments, Zen 6 execution on 2-nanometer technology and improving supply visibility.
AMD's fiscal third-quarter revenue rose 45% year-over-year to $13.4 billion, while data-center revenue surged 97% to $8.5 billion, driven by strong sales of EPYC processors and Instinct graphics processing units (GPUs).
Management expects fourth-quarter revenue of around $17 billion, implying 66% year-over-year growth at the midpoint.
William Blair nevertheless flagged competition from custom application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), particularly at Meta Platforms (META) and OpenAI, as a risk to AMD's Instinct business. However, the firm sees these custom chip programs creating additional opportunities for AMD's server CPUs, per the Investing.com report.
On Stocktwits, retail investors' sentiment around AMD stock remained in the 'extremely bullish' territory amid high user message volume.
So far this year, AMD's share price has more than doubled, surging by over 147%. In comparison, the Invesco NASDAQ 100 ETF (QQQM) and the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK), which hold the stock, have risen 12% and 21%, respectively, over the same period.
