articles.title_orig: An Expert And A Noob Play ‘Final Fantasy Resonance’
articles.title_zh: An Expert And A Noob Play ‘Final Fantasy Resonance’
articles.content_orig:
9:53 AM EST on November 12, 2026
While there are many fantastic Japanese role-playing game (JRPG, for short) series out there, and with apologies to Dragon Quest and Persona , Final Fantasy is the biggest and most important of them all. Every numbered entry in the main series is an event, and since almost every game is its own story (to date, there have been two main games to get direct sequels: X got X-2 , and XIII inexplicably got two sequels), there are swaths of new gamers dipping in every time a new game releases.
Despite that, it's safe to say that Final Fantasy has somewhat lost its way, or at least what was once its identity. What started as a turn-based RPG has evolved, first into a more active-style combat system and then more recently into something bordering on an action game. This makes sense for Square Enix, the series's developer, as turn-based combat has mostly, though not entirely, slipped from an important game genre into something more niche. Chasing the action trend that took over turn-based RPG's spot with the Soulsborne games made financial sense, and it kept Final Fantasy from growing stale.
That said, there's still a hunger for turn-based RPGs, and especially turn-based Final Fantasy games; the last mainline game to be strictly turn-based was 2001's X . With that in mind, we arrive at Final Fantasy Resonance , the recently released (and relatively successful) spin-off that is a sort of remake/re-using of assets of Final Fantasy Brave Exvius , a mobile gacha game. Resonance is not asking the player to part with any money besides the initial price tag, and instead is a fully fleshed-out 30-to-40-hour turn-based RPG adventure through time, space, and Final Fantasy history.
As a Final Fantasy devotee, I (Luis) was beyond hyped to play Resonance upon its release, but I also knew that this would be the type of game that I could convince people to play if they had any passing interest in JRPGs. Enter Barry "Baby Gamer" Petchesky, who has grown into quite the Real Gamer since he first blogged his post-pandemic gaming habits. I knew that Barry had played and enjoyed another Square Enix JRPG series, and I knew that he appreciated the HD-2D style of visuals that Resonance would employ. (For those who do not know, HD-2D visuals utilize 2D character graphics within fully 3D environments.) Since Resonance takes a journey through Final Fantasy games past, I was curious how someone with no relationship to the series would experience the game compared to someone like me, who has played almost every game in the series. As it turns out, we had very different experiences playing Final Fantasy Resonance , but somehow arrived at very similar conclusions about what the game actually felt like to play.
What's your previous experience with JRPGs broadly, and Final Fantasy specifically?
Barry: I was never a JRPG guy. As a kid, and also as an adult but slightly less so, I was a very impulsive gamer. I didn’t have the patience for a game where I might have to strategize ahead, or would need to “waste” a turn on healing my party when I could just attack again. So I would just not ever heal. As you might imagine, this made turn-based RPGs far more difficult for me than they needed to be, so I didn’t enjoy them, so I didn’t play them. I think I brute-forced my way through Secret of Mana and Super Mario RPG and that’s about it. And then once I left for college I stopped playing games altogether until I picked it back up during the pandemic. Several whole generations of game design came and went without me paying attention.
From what I’ve played/observed as an adult, JRPGs have largely felt like they are Not For Me. I’m still not a strategy guy, and the conventions of the genre—what I once referred to as “anime bullshit” but have come to understand is actually better termed “JRPG bullshit"—are a big turn-off. You know the stuff: template character designs, crude sexualization of female characters, irritating English voice acting, disjointed plotting, and the fact that seemingly every game’s story does in fact come down to “using the power of friendship to kill God.”
I am still not a JRPG guy. But what I am is an Octopath Traveler guy. I was convinced to try it by reading one particular review of OT2, which raved about its HD-2D art style (which is indeed beautiful), but more importantly mentioned how the eight different plots run the gamut from traditional JRPG god-killing to lower-stakes quests. Lower stakes is what I want! That felt new and appealing to me, and yes, I found myself most invested in the characters who had the least on the line. Agnea, my queen, I’m so glad I could help you succeed in your quest to become a famous dancer. Ultimately, OT2 won me over by being gorgeous to look at, requiring zero grinding (a non-starter for me), and having combat mechanisms that were simple enough for me to grasp yet rewarding to nail.
Luis: I am on the complete opposite side of the JRPG spectrum. Ever since I played Final Fantasy IX on my cousin's PS1, I have been obsessed with the series and with the genre as a whole. I've even written about it deep in COVID quarantine psychosis . The things that you say are Not For You—buffing, healing, strategy, anime/JRPG bullshit—all hit the spot for me. I wouldn't call myself a connoisseur of the genre, as there are so, so, sooooo many series I haven't even dipped my toes into (I will get to the Trails series before I die, though). But I think I can call myself an expert on Final Fantasy at least.
It's interesting to me that it was Octopath Traveler that hooked you. I've played both OT1 and OT2 and I found them both to be ... fine. The lack of interconnectivity in the first one put me off; it just felt like eight separate stories were happening in orbit with each other and nothing more. The second one improves that, but I still found it exhausting to have to do eight semi-tutorial introductions before moving on. (I know I could have done them in a different order, but I am a completionist.) The combat was also acceptable but nothing spectacular; we'll get to it, but I much preferred Resonance and its stagger mechanic to the break system in the Octopath games. If there's one thing that I do love about that series, though, it's the HD-2D look; after playing the first one, all I wanted was for a proper Final Fantasy game in the style, and here we are.
How did you feel about the combat in Resonance ?
Barry : I played on normal, because I read beforehand that “normal” was pretty easy. And it was. Not so much that I could get away with not having an active healer in my party, but that’s OK; I’m an adult now and can pass the marshmallow test. It was, however, easy enough that I could mostly skip using buffs. I used Nichol for the chapter he was introduced, then never used him again. I could see, vaguely, how there were possibilities in there to break the game, but I don’t really consider video game combat a puzzle to be solved, like I know some people do. Maybe because I fear that if I solve it, it’ll remove all drama from the game going forward.
On the whole, the combat was a satisfying loop. I liked having to figure out an enemy’s elemental weakness (something I assume is common in JRPGs but which I have only ever personally encountered in the Octopath games), using that weakness to whittle down their stagger bar, and then unleashing hell on a defenseless enemy (another Octopathian rhythm, to me). But I did miss the “boost point” system from Octopath which added a third variable to combat, in letting you save up what are effectively damage multipliers. Sorry, I know I sound like the guy who has only ever seen Boss Baby .
But a funny thing happened about halfway through the game. By then I had leveled up enough, or maybe just gotten the hang of things enough, that combat had become too easy. This is counterintuitive, but it made me turn the difficulty down even more, to the easiest setting. I wasn’t in danger of dying to anyon

articles.title_orig: Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395
articles.title_zh: Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395
articles.content_orig:
Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance. Not only is propping a computer up on your nose an uncomfortable proposition, but the privacy aspect has been vexing people since the Google Glass days . Now, Google is ready to take another swing at “ intelligent eyewear ” for the Gemini era after previewing its plans a couple of times. The first glasses are up for preorder today from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but they’re no impulse buy.
These devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers. Gentle Monster and Warby Parker have each designed a few different frames, with options for transparent and tinted lenses. Samsung is providing the computing hardware that fits inside them, and Google has the software covered.
Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above). They are available with both standard optical and sun lenses in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colors at $395 and higher. Warby Parker is only selling devices in the US. Gentle Monster has gone a bit further with six styles, but Google hasn’t told us any names for those yet. They come in dark red, pink, gray, and yellow colors and are available with clear, tinted, blue, or brown lenses. The Gentle Monster styles start a little higher at $449, and they will be available in the US and South Korea.
Google says the frames all weigh about 41 grams, which is not terrible but is definitely near the top for glasses generally. They will, naturally, weigh much more when you account for lenses. That will also determine the final pricing. So far, we only have the starting prices for these devices, including non-prescription lenses.
The setup here is similar to the Ray-Ban Meta glasses we’ve seen for a few years. There are no screens in the lenses, but you can interact with the AI system via voice or by activating the integrated camera. The experience should be similar to using Gemini Live on your phone, but it will be a lot easier to fire up the AI. You can say “Hey Gemini” or tap a touch-sensitive area of the frame to start interacting with the robot.
Credit:
                                      Gentle Monster Credit:

          
          Gentle Monster
Since this is the same chatbot that operates across the Google ecosystem, it has access to your data and preferences. You can ask questions and get personalized answers, have Google Maps guide you by voice, or just talk with the AI to kill time. The glasses use custom open-ear speakers to limit distractions for those around you. Google notes the directional microphones should not pick up speech from other people, either.
Adding the camera feed is where things get interesting. When the AI can see what you see, it has the potential to do more work on your behalf. Google suggests asking Gemini for recommendations when looking at a bookshelf or glancing at an event poster to have the AI add it to your calendar. The glasses will also support Gemini Guided Vision, which provides conversational audio descriptions for people who are visually impaired.
The utility of these devices hinges on Gemini. I would be remiss not to point out that Gemini, like all AI systems, is not infallible. In fact, it can be frustratingly fallible at times. The chatbot still regularly screws up simple things like adding calendar appointments or identifying objects in an image in my testing, and when you don’t have a screen to verify the AI’s output, it may be harder to trust it. These devices will really only make sense if you can rely on Gemini to do things right, and that’s still not a guarantee.
All the Gemini-powered glasses from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker feature a 12 MP wide-angle camera capable of shooting photos and video. Google says it has implemented a number of features and limitations to ensure people don’t do creepy things with its intelligent eyewear, and that it doesn’t do creepy things to you—Google claims its approach respects privacy on “both sides of the lens.”
For starters, there’s a recording light that is on whenever the camera is active. Like the Meta glasses, Google’s eyewear will detect if the light has been covered up or modified in any way that would prevent it from illuminating. In that event, the glasses will refuse to activate the camera. All Google-powered glasses will have a physical off switch, too.
Credit:
                                      Warby Parker Credit:

          
          Warby Parker
The terms of use for Gemini eyewear also require users to agree not to record people without consent or in sensitive areas. If Google finds out someone has broken those rules, it may remotely disable the glasses. Google is going a bit further in restricting video functionality than Meta, too. Google says it will not allow any apps in the Play Store to live stream video to social media from the glasses (not even YouTube live is supported). The content you record is saved to your gallery, and you can upload that wherever you want, but going live is apparently not on the agenda. Real-time facial recognition is also off the table, according to Google.  The glasses also automatically redact faces before sending video to Google for processing.
On the user privacy side, Google says it will not save any images or videos captured by the glasses in your Gemini history. Additionally, none of that data will be used for training AI models or targeting ads. Your voice interactions with Gemini via the glasses are, as with all other Gemini endpoints, not guaranteed the same level of protection. You can delete your chats from the Gemini history, though.
Data on the glasses is encrypted, and it remains that way during transit to the cloud. However, it’s not encrypted on Google’s servers. The company does note that it’s working to bring Private AI Compute to glasses, which will isolate data during processing so not even Google can access it.
Credit:
                                      Gentle Monster Credit:

          
          Gentle Monster
Anyone looking to get Gemini on their face and test Google’s privacy promise can preorder the glasses from the Gentle Monster and Warby Parker websites. Devices should ship and appear on store shelves on December 10. Importantly, support for these devices is a bit narrow at launch. They will work with all iPhones from the 13 Pro onward. On the Android side, you’ll need a Pixel 7 or newer or a Samsung Galaxy S or Z series device running One UI 9 or later. If you’ve got a cheaper Samsung Galaxy or a device from another OEM, you’re out of luck at the moment.

articles.title_orig: Spain: Housing crisis prompts first general strike in 14 years, before hundreds of thousands join protest
articles.title_zh: Spain: Housing crisis prompts first general strike in 14 years, before hundreds of thousands join protest
articles.content_orig:
Watch: Protesters and police clash in Barcelona
Clashes have broken out between groups of masked men and police in Barcelona after tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike for 14 years, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living.
Some 120,000 people joined a demonstration in the capital Madrid and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, where footage showed masked men setting fire to rubbish bins and smashing shop windows as police fired tear gas.
Transport and other public services across Spain faced serious disruption.
Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.
The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Ãlvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."
There was a heavy police presence in the centre of Barcelona on Wednesday evening, with officers wearing helmets and riot shields.
Some of the disturbances took place in the Passeig de GrÃ cia, close to the iconic PlaÃ§a de Catalunya in the centre of the city.
Small fires burned in the middle of the streets as bins were set alight. Local media reported that a group of people fired fireworks towards police and looted shops including the Lego store. Protesters were also seen trying to enter the Apple Store.
The BBC spoke to a woman who attended the protests in Barcelona who said it was mostly very peaceful and "joyful".  She said she was there to protest about the housing costs and that "there were a lot of children and old people there."
She was in the area of Las Ramblas in the evening and saw fires in the streets.  "The fires were everywhere, it was very intense," she said.
Earlier in the day there was major disruption around Madrid and Barcelona, with traffic halted on several main roads.
The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices.
Police said they had made dozens of arrests
"We've completely brought the city to a standstill," a protester in Madrid told Reuters news agency, adding there was widespread support for the general strike. "Everyone's out there, despite the rainy weather; everyone's out on the streets."
Another protester, 37-year-old teacher Olga Domingo, said she was protesting because "the housing situation is outrageous. The current cost of living compared to wages is completely unsustainable".
The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later.
Rental prices in the capital have risen in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50 sq m apartment in Madrid was an average of â¬1,170 ($1,300; Â£1,000) in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about â¬2,460.
That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions.
Watch: Protesters gather across Spain for first general strike in 14 years
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform.
Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes.
And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. SÃ¡nchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing.
"Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcareâ¦ These were collective conquests," he wrote on social media, praising those who took part in previous strikes.
Tyres were set on fire in the city of Gijon in northern Spain
The conservative People's Party (PP), by contrast, has accused the government of attempting to weaponise the strike for electoral gain.
PP leader Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o called the general strike "nonsense", calling the unions "mafia" and "trash". Feijoo's party is leading in the polls and party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed, which looks the most likely outcome of the 29 November election.
SÃ¡nchez told Spanish TV this week: "What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike."
Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Ãlvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid.
Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights.
The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.
Ãlvarez knew the 87-year-old, who had faced a tripling of her rent under new landlords, and says he was deeply upset by her treatment.
He rents a small, one-bedroom flat with his girlfriend, a dental hygienist, in the city's southern Arganzuela disrict. The couple pay â¬1,000 between them, which means each spends about half of their salary on housing, even before other bills.
"It's absolutely crazyâ¦ with the food, with the electricity, with the water, with gas."
He sees no way of getting on the property ladder: "You have to collect an insane amount of money to be able to buy a house. So with these salaries, it's impossible."
With current rent and purchase prices, he believes buying somewhere is "completely impossible".
Gonzalo Ãlvarez, who was taking part in the general strike, says 50% of his salary goes towards rent
However, the vice-president of the CEOE, Spanish biggest business association, Miguel Garrido, criticised the strike, complaining that businesses had little to do with the price of housing.
"This is not a strike for labour-related reasons, but rather for political ones, and it is closely linked to the early calling of elections," he said.
Demonstrations were planned for some of Spain's biggest cities later in the day and the scale of support will be widely viewed as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election.
Another reliable indicator of support for strikes is the level of demand for electricity with Spain's industrial sector.
Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red ElÃ©ctrica. During the last general strike 14 years ago, equivalent consumption was down by more than 15%.
Additional reporting by Gabriela Pomeroy
The general strike took place little more than two weeks ahead of national elections in Spain

articles.title_orig: Singapore barred Alice Huang for giving police ‘inaccurate information’
articles.title_zh: Singapore barred Alice Huang for giving police ‘inaccurate information’
articles.content_orig:
Singapore’s government said on Thursday the United States had provided little help in its investigation into Alice Huang, the woman at the center of a spy plot that has led to the investigation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang .
Singaporean authorities held Ms. Huang’s passport to prevent her from leaving the country from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” in relation to her company, Megaspeed, which is based in the country, the government said in a statement. She was ultimately released with a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore.
The statement raises new questions about the response of the Trump administration to the case and why the U.S. government did not more forcefully intervene. According to the timeline in the statement, Singaporean authorities had been holding Ms. Huang’s passport well after President Trump was briefed last fall about her relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive and the belief that she was a Chinese intelligence asset.
The New York Times has reported that Taiwan began monitoring Ms. Huang in 2024 at the guidance of the U.S. government.
In its statement, Singapore said that it had sought information from an American server maker and close Nvidia business partner, Supermicro, but that the company had been uncooperative. Supermicro, a firm that packages Nvidia’s A.I. chips onto servers that can be used in data centers, has been at the center of a number of chip smuggling investigations across the globe.
Supermicro was a supplier to Megaspeed, a company incorporated in Singapore and run by Ms. Huang, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.
Singapore said in the statement its authorities raised Supermicro’s “limited cooperation” with the U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation in July 2025 and “requested their assistance in securing the company’s cooperation.”
“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement said.
Supermicro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
During questioning, Ms. Huang sought to downplay her role in Megaspeed, according to Singapore’s statement. She was ultimately released because of “insufficient evidence relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.”
She was issued a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore. The country’s police are continuing to investigate Megaspeed.
Paul Mozur is the global technology correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei. Previously he wrote about technology and politics in Asia from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Seoul.

articles.title_orig: Help! A Broken Toilet Grounded My Plane, and the Airline Won’t Cover a Hotel.
articles.title_zh: Help! A Broken Toilet Grounded My Plane, and the Airline Won’t Cover a Hotel.
articles.content_orig:
On May 30, my wife and I were scheduled to take Turkish Airlines’ evening flight from Denver to Istanbul. The flight was delayed several hours because of what we were told was a mechanical problem. We boarded the aircraft at around 11:30 p.m., taxied to the runway and then returned to the gate. The flight was finally canceled at around 1 a.m. Gate agents advised us that no hotel vouchers were available and that we should find hotels and submit our receipts to the airline. We stayed at the airport Westin, paying $512, including taxes and breakfast, and flew out the next day. We heard — and later read in The Denver Post — that the cancellation had been caused by an overflowing lavatory. But the airline sent us a message attributing the disruption to “force majeure,” which to me means an earthquake or a war or something similar. I called the airline and was told to submit my hotel receipts online, which I did twice, but got no response. Turkish Airlines’ customer service plan says the carrier pays for hotels only if the reason for the cancellation was under its control. Is Turkish evading responsibility with this “force majeure” argument? Can you help? Neal, Broomfield, Colo.
How an airline describes the cause of a cancellation can directly affect whether it will cover passengers’ lodging, transportation and meals. For mechanical issues, the answer is often yes; for weather or air-traffic issues, it’s almost always no.
U.S. regulations define those categories, but they do not require airlines to pay for stranded passengers’ expenses. Nevertheless, all the major U.S. carriers except Frontier explicitly promise hotel stays in their customer service plans if the reason for the disruption is under their control. The Turkish Airlines policy for U.S. flights is a bit looser — but the airline usually offers lodging for controllable disruptions.
For the last couple of years, I’ve kept a file of emails from travelers who suspected, as you do, that a carrier had weaseled its way out of covering passengers’ expenses by misrepresenting what happened.
I had avoided the ever-expanding file because I knew that proving the precise cause of any one incident was most likely a fool’s errand. Disruptions can have multiple causes, and the U.S. Department of Transportation gives the airlines flexibility in determining the main one. For example, if a mechanical problem causes a delay, then a storm moves in and shuts down the airport, airlines can blame the weather. No hotel voucher for you!
But the evidence in your case seemed pretty overwhelming. When airlines cite force majeure, they are generally referring to extraordinary circumstances beyond their control — like a natural disaster. The Denver Post article had the headline “Turkish Airlines Cancels Flight From Denver Airport After Urine and Feces Erupt From Plane’s Toilet,” which is disgusting but hardly earthquake-level terrible. Citing force majeure seemed like, at best, an entertaining error or, at worst, an attempt to avoid compensating passengers for their hotels, a promise you said gate agents made at the time.

articles.title_orig: The Nvidia Board Members Who Will Decide Jensen Huang’s Fate
articles.title_zh: The Nvidia Board Members Who Will Decide Jensen Huang’s Fate
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, a 13-year company veteran, is taking the helm of the world's most valuable chipmaker on an interim basis after Jensen Huang's sudden resignation.
"She's the only one internally that has this significant respect," Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC before the news had been made official. "She's more than just a CFO. I'd almost view her as more of a COO."
Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation
Nvidia hasn't announced a succession plan and said the board is considering internal and external candidates.
Kress joined Nvidia in September 2013, after holding finance roles at Cisco , Microsoft and Texas Instruments . At Nvidia, Kress has been the other big voice on earnings calls, reporting the company's results and taking questions alongside Huang.
"NVIDIA's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said in Thursday's statement . "We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, was known for running the company with no clear second-in-command, personally deciding which projects are a priority and emailing engineers about details.
But when it came to Kress, "Jensen didn't do anything without her," Ives said. "She's a Swiss Army knife for Nvidia. Anything strategically: customers, partners, technology. She was involved."
CNBC spoke to nearly a dozen Nvidia insiders and former Kress co-workers. They described her as savvy, knowledgeable, thoughtful and clear-headed.
Kress is stepping in at a moment of crisis. Huang has operated as Nvidia's spokesperson, the face of the company and a founder synonymous with the brand. He also pioneered the artificial intelligence chip industry, making him the central figure in the multitrillion-dollar boom that's driving the U.S. economy.
Kress "deeply understands the business and has shown fierce loyalty to the company," Daniel Newman, CEO of Futurum Group, wrote in a message to CNBC.
Nvidia shares plunged 14% on Thursday after the announcement. The stock is poised for its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest slump since 2012. The shares have been dragged down by broad concerns about the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats.
Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday.
The Huang saga burst into public view on Sunday, when the CEO apologized for being unfaithful to his wife. That followed reports that he'd had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence suspects is a spy. Pressure intensified late Wednesday after The New York Times reported a second affair, this one with an employee named Kimberly Powell.
Kress was recognized in May as one of Fortune's most powerful women in business. Her LinkedIn profile lists her location as Saratoga, California, a wealthy city 16 miles south of Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters.
As for the long-term leadership plan, Ives said Kress will likely serve for about a year as interim CEO but the permanent replacement will come from outside the company.
"You need someone that's been on the global stage," Ives said. "Given the importance of the company not just in the U.S. tech industry but the global economy."
— CNBC's Seema Mody and Jordan Novet contributed to this report

Below is a roundup of developments from the Ukraine-Russia talks on Thursday, November 12:
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have concluded meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and will now travel to Dublin, Ireland, where they will meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy who is attending a European summit there.
Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, described talks with Putin as "substantive and detailed."
He and Witkoff were in Moscow after two-days of talks in Abu Dhabi seeking to find a way to end Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine.
In Moscow, however, Putin showed no inclination toward compromise, saying that he would no back off of his territorial demands, while at the same time rejecting proposals to station foreign peacekeeping troops in  Ukraine, dismissing such a deployment as a "continuation of war."
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed their trip to Abu Dhabi this week with Russian President Vladimir Putin .
According to Russian state media RIA Novosti, Witkoff said US President Donald Trump was "seeking to end the conflict in Ukraine as quickly as possible."
The three-way talks in Abu Dhabi between the US, Ukraine and Russia were held "in a positive atmosphere" and that the Ukrainian and Russian delegations had "worked effectively," Ria Novosti reported.
Witkoff said he would convey the results of his and Kushner's meeting with Putin to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
Kushner, for his part, said the US had begun discussions with European countries on the post-war "security architecture" on the continent.
He also said Europe wanted to be involved in the talks to end the conflict, RIA Novosti reported.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a "humanitarian mission" to the frontline city of Kostyantynivka in eastern Ukraine, Russian state media reported.
Putin made the remarks during a meeting at the Kremlin on Thursday with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Ria Novosti said.
"There's a village in Donbas called Kostyantynivka, where there are still about 400-500 civilians. Let's do the same thing we did in Oleshky and invite representatives of the foreign press, including the American press," he said, referring to the recent US-brokered evacuation of the Russia-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine .
According to RIA Novosti, Putin also repeated Russia's demands in a potential peace deal, including its refusal to accept any foreign troops in Ukraine.
The Russian leader warned that international peacekeepers in Ukraine would become a "legitimate target for the Russian army."
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Russian side is becoming more willing to accept a European seat in the trilateral talks.
Merz said he expected Putin to agree to Europeans getting a seat at the table in talks with Ukraine. He was speaking on the sidelines of the European Political Community meeting in Dublin. He added that getting Putin to negotiate is more important than naming who would be the European envoy.
"The important thing is that Russia comes to the table and that Russia is ready to talk," the German chancellor said.
He also highlighted Ukraine's importance to Europe, saying that supporting Kyiv was a "shared European responsibility."
For some time, European leaders have sought a seat at the US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi. So far, representatives from the EU were only present on the sidelines of the talks.
Ukraine's military said on Thursday it ‌has hit ⁠Russia's five ​largest oil ​refineries since ​October 30.
Those struck were the Omsk, Kirishi, Ryazan, Nizhny Novgorod and Yaroslavl refineries, along with the smaller Novokuibyshevsk and Saratov refineries, the General Staff said in a Telegram post.
The statement claimed that the strikes on key refining units are shrinking revenues that help Russia fund the war.
Referring to the Omsk refinery's distance of 2,500 kilometers (1,553 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Last month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that military strikes on Russian energy infrastructure would resume, despite US President Donald Trump's insistence that such attacks stop.
Trump said Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries were a "disgrace" and that Zelenskyy was less willing than Putin to reach a compromise to end the war.
Russia , however, has paid no heed to Trump, instead continuing to hit Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure.

Leaders from more than 40 European countries will gather in the Irish capital Dublin on Thursday for the European Political Community summit to discuss the continent's security and Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will also attend the meeting, along with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
US mediators, Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump , and special envoy Steve Witkoff are also expected to make their way to Ireland, after their meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
The meeting, due to begin at midday local time, is an opportunity for European leaders to discuss this week's trilateral peace talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday that Ukraine's military faced new "systematic restrictions" to tech billionaire Elon Musk's Starshield satellite internet.
"Our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now," Zelenskyy said in an online post.
The Ukrainian president added that "systematic speed restrictions" were being imposed and that these are not "random errors."
"Unfortunately, this is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine."
The Starshield military communications system — the military-grade version of satellite-based communication network Starlink — is operated by Musk's SpaceX and plays a key role for frontline communications.
Ukraine first flagged issues with Starshield last month after a dispute between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump over a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk "capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network."
Tech billionaire and US president both denied throttling Ukrainian access, but Musk later accused Ukraine of using the service for military purposes while Trump said Musk had "put it back."
Nearly half a million Russian soldiers may have been killed in Vladimir Putin 's war in Ukraine. Can Russia continue fighting at such an enormous human and economic cost?
Leaked records reportedly obtained from Russia's state statistics agency, Rosstat, identify more than 412,000 deaths linked to the war. British newspaper The Guardian reports that the true death toll could be closer to 500,000.
The full dataset has not been independently verified.
Some months saw more than 500 Russian soldiers killed every day. And the losses have fallen disproportionately on Russia's poorer and more remote regions.
In this DW News interview, Janis Kluge, head of the Eastern Europe and Eurasia research division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), examines what the leaked figures reveal about Russia's military losses, recruitment crisis and war economy.
The leaked data comes as US-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine conclude in Abu Dhabi without a breakthrough on ending the war.
The two sides have agreed to a prisoner exchange, but fundamental disagreements remain. Could mounting Russian losses eventually force Putin to compromise, or make him even more determined to continue the war?

articles.title_orig: Apple HomeView Review: A Versatile Smart Display And Siri-Powered Home Hub
articles.title_zh: Apple HomeView Review: A Versatile Smart Display And Siri-Powered Home Hub
articles.content_orig:
The company’s smart screen debut heavily relies on an iPhone or iPad — for better and for worse.
Apple's entry into the smart display category was rumored for years. By the time its debut home hub device arrives this week, the company will be nearly a decade behind its main rivals in the space. In true Apple fashion, it refused to rush new products just because most of the competition was doing it. Now that the HomeView ($299) is here, Apple is hoping the iPhone faithful will like its mix of elevated design and newly expanded Siri capabilities .
Unlike smart displays from Amazon and Google, Apple's approach relies on a companion device. That means you'll need either an iPhone or an iPad to mirror apps using technology similar to CarPlay. As you'd imagine, that means the HomeView's usefulness, like CarPlay's, is directly tied to how much you use Apple's core apps — things like Messages, Calendar, Photos, Reminders and others. You'll also need to have some smart home devices to make the most of the smart display and be willing to use Safari as your recipe box. If all of that is OK to you, and if you're willing to give Siri access to personal data inside some of those apps, the HomeView can quickly become a very versatile device with something for your whole family.
I have fond memories of the iMac G4 . It was the first computer I used in a design lab in college, and I loved how I could reposition the display to suit the task at hand. The first time I saw the HomeView, those memories flooded back. Apple's smart home display doesn't exactly replicate the G4 styling, but it's close enough for a decent nostalgia hit for me.
The HomeView essentially consists of two parts: a cylindrical, domed base and a 7-inch Liquid Retina display. At least, that's if you get the tabletop version. The wall-mounted option is just the screen, and you'll have to pay at least $59.95 for a mount. Every version of the HomeView has two full-range drivers in the display itself. The base houses additional components, like a down-firing woofer and a pair of force-canceling passive radiators for fuller sound with more bass than the wall-mounted models.
That display has an LED-backlit multi-touch IPS panel that offers a 1,088 x 1,088 resolution at 200 pixels per inch. Apple says it also added an oleophobic fingerprint-resistant coating to cut down on grime from everyday use. There's an ambient light sensor that enables the HomeView to adjust both brightness and warmth as needed. If it's in direct sunlight, you can expect the maximum 500 nits, but at night, it can dial things down to just 0.3 nits — the lowest brightness ever on an Apple display. The company believes this makes it perfect for a nightstand, if you're willing to have a camera pointed at or near your bed.
The HomeView's display has bezels like an iPad and the shape of a large Apple Watch. Unlike either of those devices, though, it has no physical buttons for controls. All of the interaction is done via swipes and taps on the touchscreen itself, or, as I'll elaborate on in a bit, with your voice. And unlike that iMac I'm nostalgic for, you can only tilt the display — you can't adjust its height. While that will suit most of your needs, I'm sure there are a lot of people who would've liked the ability to change the height or rotate the screen as well. Once you do adjust the way it tilts, a built-in accelerometer detects the new angle and alters the audio performance of the display's two drivers to match it.
Another item to discuss in terms of design is the HomeView's lone port. Around back, there's a single USB-C jack for power. Apple ships the standard version of the device with a USB-C to USB-C cable and a 30-watt power adapter. If you opt for the USB-C wall mount, which already costs $59.99, you'll need to purchase the power adapter separately. The company offers a 40W dynamic power adapter (up to 60W max) for $39 while the minimum required power supply ( 20W ) will cost you $19. Obviously, the AC wired and PoE (power over Ethernet) wired mounts won't need a power adapter.
And lastly, there's the matter of color. For the standard (table or countertop) version of HomeView, you can choose from Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink or Space Gray options. On those, the sides and back of the display match the base. For the wall-mounted version, you can only pick between Silver and Space Gray. And, just in case you need the reminder, both HomeView models are the same price ($299).
One of the HomeView's most helpful traits is its ability to put Siri AI front and center in your home. The smart device runs on Apple's A18 chip, the processor that debuted with the iPhone 16 line in 2024. The company is using it here for its Secure Exclaves which give it the ability to process camera and microphone feeds on-device in a manner that can't be accessed by Apple. The company explained that this enables the HomeView to recognize your face and voice, or that of other users in your home, without exposing any of the data to the operating system.
That's important, because Siri AI now has access to more of your personal data, like your conversations in Messages, info from your Calendar invites and other bits of "personal context" from various apps. Of course, you have to opt-in to all of this by enabling Apple Intelligence on your iPhone or iPad, and you can limit which apps Siri can index data from. If you do decide to use the system, I can attest that it works well on the HomeView, though it's merely another vessel for the larger AI system.
During a lengthy conversation about lighthouses in North Carolina, Siri gave me information about visiting a variety of locations in the state. It provided information that I didn't specifically ask for, like which ones were still active, and got more comprehensive when my follow-up query was a bit vague. For example, when I asked "Which lighthouse is the easiest to get to?" Siri responded with both a list of ones you can park close to and highlighted the one that requires the least amount of climbing.
Siri was able to check my calendar to see if I was free to take the trip on a certain date and provided travel time from my house (including follow-up questions about the cities I'd pass through). I was finally able to stump the AI when I asked about "good hotels" near the Currituck Beach Lighthouse in Corolla, but even still, things felt more natural and conversational than interactions I've had with Siri in the past.
At times, Siri showed text answers on the HomeView in addition to reciting the info. When I asked about driving time or my schedule, a preview of the best route and the specific day on my calendar popped up respectively. What's more, I got a notification on my phone from the Home app letting me know Siri responded to a request for personal content. But it's important to remember that HomeView is just a conduit for Siri AI and its newly expanded abilities. These same things can be done on an iPhone or other compatible Apple devices, meaning you don't really have to spend $300 on a dedicated display for these tools.
One final note on security: Since the HomeView is heavily reliant on an iPhone or iPad, those devices must be nearby and recently unlocked (and enrolled in the shared home) for Siri to access personal data. The HomeView uses facial and voice recognition to know who's speaking, and to know when they walk away, so prying eyes can't see your texts if they rush over after you've been looking at Messages or other potentially sensitive apps. Guests or family members who don't have an iPhone or iPad can still use basic functions (control smart home devices, check weather, play music, etc), including asking Siri rudimentary questions.
When I first spent time with the HomeView last month, the feature I was most excited about was the recipe integration in Safari. I'm happy to report that feeling remains, for the most part, but there's one caveat that does impact the overall experience.

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave Stock Dives. Nvidia's Huang Issue Spells Trouble for Other AI Plays.
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave Stock Dives. Nvidia's Huang Issue Spells Trouble for Other AI Plays.
articles.content_orig:
A drop for Nvidia’s stock is pulling the U.S. market lower Thursday, threatening to upend the boom in artificial intelligence technology that carried Wall Street to record after record in recent years.
The S&P 500 fell 0.6% in its latest yo-yo move. The weakness for AI stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down 0.9%, but the rest of the market was holding up better. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down a modest 15 points, or less than 0.1%, as of 9:35 a.m. Eastern time.
Nvidia’s stock dropped 9.7% following the resignation of Jensen Huang, its CEO, co-founder and face of the brand. The chip company’s stock has been sinking since its board announced an investigation into Huang for a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese government agent.
It’s a stunning fall for Nvidia, which had become Wall Street’s most valuable and influential stock because of its central role in the artificial intelligence boom. Its stock price set a record high last month after soaring an astounding 1,722% in four years. That compares with the already healthy gain of nearly 109% for the overall S&P 500 over the same time.
But Nvidia’s price dropped 27% from then through Wednesday on worries about whether Huang would remain and how Nvidia would navigate a future without him. Nvidia’s board answered the first question Thursday morning, when it said Huang resigned, and it named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as its interim CEO.
The second question remains to be determined. And it looms over the entire market because Nvidia and the broader AI industry have been the main reasons the U.S. stock market has set so many records in recent years.
Wall Street’s immediate reaction on Thursday was to punish stocks across the AI industry, though some of Nvidia’s rivals held up better in hopes of a competitive advantage.
CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, fell 10.9%. Micron Technology, which sells memory for computers that’s been getting gobbled up in the AI frenzy, sank 3.1%. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centers, slipped 0.8%.
But Broadcom rose 5.2%, and Advanced Micro Devices added 2%. They were two of the strongest forces limiting the S&P 500's losses.
Stocks also felt some pressure after President Donald Trump said he’s no longer interested in a deal with Iran to end their war, which briefly sent oil prices, worries about inflation and Treasury yields jumping. Instead of that, Trump said he asked his vice president to focus on investigating U.S. cities and states run by Democrats.
“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump said on his social-media platform. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil suddenly went from about $92 to more than $94 following Trump’s posting, before it later eased back. It was most recently at $93.34, up 0.6%.
It’s been swinging sharply since the United States and Israel began the war with Iran in late February, bouncing between roughly $70 and $150.
In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 5.03% from 4.98% late Tuesday. Trading in the bond market had been closed Wednesday for Veterans Day.
In stock markets abroad, indexes rose modestly in Europe following a weaker finish in Asia.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1.3% for one of the world’s biggest moves.

articles.title_orig: China’s diaspora crackdown reaches deep into Europe, report finds
articles.title_zh: China’s diaspora crackdown reaches deep into Europe, report finds
articles.content_orig:
THE HAGUE — Beijing is overseeing nearly 1,250 overseas policing outposts in more than 90 countries to crack down on dissidents, according to a report by a human rights advocacy organization.
The report described Europe as a hotspot with hundreds of Beijing’s policing offices across some two dozen European countries, which it said exposed China’s growing attempts to control its diaspora.
Researchers at the Spain-based organization, Safeguard Defenders, gathered open-source evidence from the Chinese Party-state to examine the extent to which the Chinese diaspora is monitored, surveilled and policed around the world.
These policing outposts “act as the Chinese Communist Party operatives for community surveillance and enforcement abroad,” according to the report.
The report lands at an awkward time for Europe’s trade officials. Ditte Juul Jørgensen, head of the EU’s trade department — which has been working to balance the trade relationship with Beijing — will meet with China’s Vice Minister of Commerce Ling Ji in Brussels on Thursday.
Europe is attempting to walk a fine line with its relations with Beijing. EU legislation proposed in January seeks to kick risky Chinese suppliers out of Europe’s most critical industries over cybersecurity concerns, while supply chain dependencies and political coercion remain ongoing challenges. The EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas has also raised concerns about what she said was China’s enabling of Russia’s war in Ukraine and credible reports of China training Russia’s military .
The report builds on initial revelations from Safeguard Defenders in 2022 that identified more than 100 facilities around the world, which the NGO described as overseas outposts of China’s security apparatus. Back then, that report said Beijing announced its “first batch” of “30 overseas police service stations in 25 cities in 21 countries.”
Following the revelations, some governments denounced the overseas police stations as illegal, and some pursued criminal investigations, the NGO said in its latest report. In response, Beijing claimed the stations had been closed, it added.
“Far from closing, the evidence shows expansion: today more than 10 police forces from five Chinese provinces work through a global network of Chinese Communist Party operatives abroad,” the new report says.
The latest paper was presented at a conference hosted by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (IPAC), a gathering of 52 cross-party lawmakers from 30 countries that campaigns for a more coordinated response to the Chinese Communist Party. Policymakers raised numerous concerns at the event in The Hague earlier this month — about what they considered security threats of critical infrastructure, trade dependencies and potential risks from a future conflict between China and Taiwan that would disrupt shipping.
The Chinese foreign ministry and state media have previously called IPAC an “anti-China” group and accused it of spreading disinformation and interfering in China’s internal affairs, particularly over Taiwan.
China’s Ministry for Foreign Affairs and its European Union mission didn’t respond to requests for comment on the report. China has previously denied running overseas police stations and says it doesn’t interfere in other countries’ internal affairs and that it respects international law.
In 2023, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson rejected the term “police stations,” saying the “institutions helped overseas Chinese who could not return to China due to the pandemic, renew their driving licence and perform physical examination.”
These 1,250 offices were “the tip of the iceberg,” according to the NGO, which said it was conservative in how it mapped and linked them to China’s policing system. To be counted, they had to be officially connected to China’s police or prosecutors and have open-source evidence of overseas activities, report author Laura Harth said. This meant broader influence or interference operations were excluded.
“All of them serve to control and instill fear in diaspora communities … all of them represent a standing national security risk,” she said.
Slovakian MEP Miriam Lexmann, who is part of the European Parliament’s trade committee and China delegation — lawmakers tasked with maintaining and managing legislative ties between the EU and China — said people needed to become more aware of the security threats posed by China.
“It means that our free countries are no longer free anymore for everyone because they are not able to guarantee freedom of speech, freedom of behavior to people who are in our country,” she told POLITICO in reference to the operations.
China’s surveillance through facial recognition and interference in communications was “the exact behavior of the former Soviet Stasi,” she said, but worse since the technology is now much more sophisticated.
The main concern expressed by lawmakers attending the IPAC conference was China’s relationship with Russia, and its help in propping up the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine. Their discussions included what this could mean for a future conflict and war on two fronts if Beijing were to try and take Taiwan militarily while NATO countries were attacked by Russia.
“The road to escalation in the Taiwan Strait can run right through what’s happening in Ukraine and in Kyiv,” said Dutch lawmaker Jan Paternotte, who co-chaired the IPAC conference.

articles.title_orig: Romanov sapphire worn by Russian empress fetches $4.9M at auction
articles.title_zh: Romanov sapphire worn by Russian empress fetches $4.9M at auction
articles.content_orig:
Morning Rundown: At least 8 dead in NYC building collapse, Jensen Huang’s fate in the balance, and Ukraine faces new Starshield disruptions
A Romanov sapphire weighing nearly 198 carats on a diamond-covered bracelet sold for more than 4.1 million Swiss francs ($4.9 million) at auction, vastly higher than the expected price range, Sotheby’s said.
The cushion-shaped sapphire attributed to onetime ownership of Russia’s imperial family was billed as a very rare stone, and had been expected to fetch between 850,000 and 1.7 million francs ($1 million and $2 million) at the Geneva auction late Wednesday.
The buyer, a private collector, wasn’t identified.
The 197.80-carat Ceylon sapphire likely came from the Mughal Empire in south Asia, made its way into Russia’s imperial jewels in the 19th century and is one of the most important surviving gemstones from the Russian court.
Dowager Empress Maria Feodorovna, Czar Nicholas II’s mother, wore the sapphire at the Winter Palace Ball of 1903 — “widely regarded as the last great spectacle of Imperial Russia and immortalized in some of the most iconic images of the Romanov court,” the auction house said.
After the Russian Revolution, the sapphire was recorded in inventory before entering the Soviet government’s dispersal sales of imperial treasures, Sotheby’s said.

articles.title_orig: Iran Update, November 11, 2026
articles.title_zh: Iran Update, November 11, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute are publishing updates Monday through Friday to provide analysis on the war with Iran and the broader Middle East. Weekday updates cover events from the past 24-hour period, whereas weekend updates are abbreviated and cover the Houthi-Saudi conflict and major breaking developments related to the war with Iran.
The US Department of Justice indicted three members of an Iranian-supported Kataib Hezbollah front group on November 10 for their involvement in nearly 20 attacks or plots in Europe and the United States, including an attempted attack on the Royal Air Force (RAF) base in Fairford in September 2026.[1] The three individuals conducted numerous attacks in Europe between March and May 2026 as part of the group known as Harakat Ashab al Yamin al Islamiya.[2] The Justice Department described Harakat Ashab al Yamin al Islamiya as a front group for Kataib Hezbollah and the IRGC.[3] Both Iran and the Iraqi militias have historically used front groups to provide plausible deniability and obfuscate their involvement in attacks and other activity.[4] The Justice Department indicted senior Kataib Hezbollah commander Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawoud al Saadi in May 2026 for his direction of Harakat Ashab al Yamin al Islamiya‘s attacks.[5] Saadi more recently organized the plot targeting RAF Fairford from prison in New York.[6] UK authorities thwarted a plot to attack US bombers stationed at the base with small explosive drones on September 27, which led the United States to relocate the bombers from the base.[7]
The front group’s pattern of activity suggests that its operations are part of an Iranian effort to compel Israel and the United States to halt attacks on Iran. The front group targeted and attempted to target numerous Jewish sites in Europe and the United States in March and April 2026, including synagogues.[8] The attacks likely aimed to retaliate against US-Israeli strikes in Iran by spreading terror and fear among US and European Jewish communities, thereby increasing the pressure on both countries to end the strike campaign. Such a strategy may reflect Iran’s recognition that previous direct Iranian attacks on Israeli soil failed to compel Israeli decisionmakers to avoid taking action against Iran.[9]
Limited US strikes on Iran in August and September, as well as reports that the United States was considering renewed strikes on Iran, may have motivated the cell’s shift from Jewish-affiliated targets to US military targets.[10]  The group paused attacks on any targets after Saadi was sentenced in the United States in May 2026. The Justice Department noted that the three men began to plan the RAF Fairford attack in August.[11] UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the House of Commons in mid-October that the IRGC ”almost certainly” directed the plot.[12] Attacks on US bases that support US operations, such as RAF Fairford, are likely intended to deter future US attacks on Iran. Iranian officials have increasingly issued threats against US bases in Europe amid expectations that the United States could imminently strike Iran again. Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei warned Arabic-language media on November 11 that Iran would target distant US bases in the event of any new attack, for example.[13] It is not clear if Rezaei is threatening to conduct direct missile or drone attacks against such bases or referring to sabotage. Several US bases in Europe lie within the range of Iran’s existing missiles.[14] The Wall Street Journal reported on November 10 that US forces relocated multiple tankers from the RAF Mildenhall Base to Germany and other countries due to an imminent threat from Iran, citing people familiar with the matter.[15]
Ansar al Furqan, a Baloch Salafi-jihadi group, has at least partially merged into the Mobarizoun Popular Front (MPF), a coalition of Baloch anti-regime groups that has conducted several operations in Sistan and Baluchistan Province in recent months.[16] The MPF claimed that the merger would unite Baloch armed groups and increase the effectiveness of anti-regime operations. [17] Jaish al Adl and several other Baloch militant groups formed the MPF in December 2025 to fight against the regime and increase coordination among anti-regime groups in southeastern Iran.[18] Ansar al Furqan did not publicly join the MPF when the coalition formed and continued to operate independently. MPF Spokesperson Mahmoud Baloch announced on November 11 that Ansar al Furqan had merged into the MPF after unspecified Baloch figures mediated between the groups.[19]  It is unclear at this time how fully Ansar al Furqan has merged into the MPF. An anti-regime Baloch media outlet subsequently reported that Ansar al Furqan spokesperson Molavi Nasrollah Baloch confirmed the full merger.[20] An alleged direct statement from Ansar al Furqan alternatively suggested that only a small number of its fighters chose to join the MPF on their own initiative and that Ansar al Furqan’s foundational structure and principal divisions remain intact.[21] The discrepancies in reporting about Ansar al Furqan‘s decision to join the MPF may reflect internal splits within the group, although available reporting does not identify the defectors or explain why they joined the MPF. This merger comes amid an uptick in anti-regime militant activity in southeastern Iran in recent months.[22]
Ansar al Furqan and the MPF share the common objective to overthrow the Iranian regime, which may explain in part Ansar al Furqan’s decision to join the MPF at this time. Ansar al Furqan called the MPF fighters its “brothers” and expressed support for their anti-regime struggle, which indicates that the groups share a common enemy despite their ideological differences.[23] The MPF’s charter identifies “deep political change” in Iran as its central objective and frames its struggle around the regime’s oppression of Baloch citizens and other Iranians.[24] The MPF has explicitly called for the overthrow of the Velayat-e Faqih [the Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist] system, but the coalition has not advocated for Baloch independence or autonomy.[25] The MPF contains Salafi-jihadi groups, such as Jaish al Adl, but the coalition itself has not expressed Salafi-jihadi views.  Ansar al Furqan also seeks the regime’s collapse but frames its campaign as jihad and emphasizes the role of religious scholars in its leadership.[26] Ansar al Furqan has used sectarian terms to refer to the Iranian regime and Shia groups, whereas the MPF promotes cooperation among Iranians across ideological divisions.[27]  Shared objectives to collapse the regime may have encouraged some fighters to join the MPF, while strict ideological adherence may have compelled other Ansar al Furqan fighters to remain independent. Ideological differences between Ansar al Furqan and the MPF could lead to disagreements over rhetoric, recruitment, or ideology that could limit the feasibility of the partnership.
The Ansar al Furqan fighters who joined the MPF may increase the coalition’s capabilities through additional manpower and combat experience. It is unclear how many Ansar al Furqan fighters have joined the MPF, however. Ansar al Furqan has conducted some tactically sophisticated attacks, including a large-scale attack against a Law Enforcement Command (LEC) checkpoint in Fahraj, Kerman Province, in December 2025.[28] The MPF has already demonstrated the ability to conduct complex operations across southeastern Iran, including a nine-hour engagement in Saravan in September and a combined improvised explosive device (IED) and small-arms attack in Jalgh in October.[29]  The impacts of Ansar al Furqan’s merger on the MPF’s capabilities will also depend on the extent to which the MPF incorporates these fighters into the MPF’s command structures.
Nothing significant to report.
Assessed Iranian War Aims:
Nothing

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Investing.com-- NVIDIA (NVDA) fell 7.8% in after hours trade on Wednesday following a report that the board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang. Read more

Shares of AMD and Broadcom rose in response, with the two being viewed as potential beneficiaries of a prolonged governance crisis at what is arguably their biggest rival.
The allegations: Huang admitted an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data-center company that is a large Nvidia customer. US intelligence reportedly suspects her of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Read more (Nov 10, 2026)
The probes: The board has opened an investigation, and Trump said the FBI is looking into it. Nvidia says it has "no reason to believe" secrets were compromised.
The damage: Over two sessions, about $427B of market value was erased. Baird downgraded the stock to neutral. Morgan Stanley dropped it from its Top Pick list, and BofA removed it from its U.S. 1 List. Read more (Nov 11, 2026)
Key-man risk: There is no succession plan. Yorkville's Dan Ives values Nvidia at $300 with Huang and $225 without . Read more
NVIDIA (NVDA): $173.73 (Market Cap: $4.20T) || 1M -23.2% || Fair value $261.16 ( +50.3% ) || Analyst target upside +82.2%
AMD (AMD): $552.90 (Market Cap: $906.8B) || 1W +36.7% , YTD +152.6% || Fair value $420.48 ( -23.9% ) || Analyst target upside +18.9%
Broadcom (AVGO): $345.22 (Market Cap: $1.65T) || 1W +18.4%, YTD -2.1% || Fair value $419.68 ( +21.6% ) || Analyst target upside +54.5%
Stop chasing stocks after they've already rallied. Find your next investment opportunity with AI stock picks, earnings insights, and market-moving news. Yahoo! Finance readers get an extra 10% off on top of the 55% off Black Friday price. Join today! »
Prices are the Nov 11 close. Fair value and analyst targets are as of Nov 11–12, 2026.
These are computed as the Nov 11 close divided by next-fiscal-year consensus EPS:
Nvidia is cheap on paper, and that is the tension. Revenue grew 65.5% last fiscal year to $215.94B, with a 71.1% gross margin. Next quarter's consensus is $108.8B in revenue and $2.47 EPS, ahead of the Nov 17 report. It beat on both lines in its last two quarters. Estimates were not cut, with EPS revisions at +5.2% over 90 days. The discount reflects governance and China risk, not weaker fundamentals. Wells Fargo still expects a revenue beat. The risk is that a CEO exit or new China export controls hit a stock already down 23% in a month.
AMD is the momentum story. Its Q3 beat on Nov 3 was EPS $2.09 vs $1.94, and the stock rose 4.7%. EPS estimates have been revised up about 10% in 30 days. Consensus has revenue rising from $52.1B (FY2026) to $95.7B (FY2027). The stock is up 152.6% YTD but still about 16% below its $658.52 high. The fair-value model sits below the price, so much of the growth is already priced in.
Broadcom is the laggard that is catching up. It is about 30% below its $495 high and down 17% over three months. Its last two prints beat estimates, yet the stock fell 13% and 3.4% afterward, which shows how high the bar is. Estimates are flat over 90 days (-0.9%). The supports are JPMorgan's view of its Google TPU role and Anthropic's compute commitment. Read more (Nov 10, 2026) Its next report is Dec 9 .
The rise in AMD and Broadcom is a rotation, not a new thesis. Hyperscaler budgets set AI spending, not Nvidia's headlines. Both stocks also rallied with the whole chip sector after a steep selloff.
Case for: Broadcom has the best setup on valuation. It trades at about 18x next-year EPS, its fair-value model shows upside, and a pullback came before this bounce. AMD has the strongest estimate momentum.
Case against: Neither stock has structurally gained from Nvidia's trouble. BofA says share gains depend on prolonged scrutiny. A quick resolution, or a strong Nov 17 report, could send money back to Nvidia. Rate risk is also growing after a hot CPI print. Read more (Nov 9, 2026)
Levels: NVIDIA (NVDA) falling below its 52-week low of $164.27 would mark a new phase of the sell-off. Broadcom (AVGO) reclaiming $350 would extend its rebound.
The data favors Broadcom's valuation setup over AMD's. Nvidia is the highest-variance case. It has the cheapest multiple and the biggest governance overhang, and there is no way to price the board's decision.

articles.title_orig: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely
articles.title_zh: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely
articles.content_orig:
A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, mod_http2 , can let a remote attacker run code on the server. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618 , it affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and is fixed in version 2.4.71, released yesterday.
Only servers with HTTP/2 enabled are affected, according to Red Hat, which ships the server as part of Red Hat Enterprise Linux.
An attacker who can reach the server needs no authentication to exploit the flaw and could take full control of the server process, the Linux vendor says. It rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale.
The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. It does not name or link that research. Security company Wiz said later that day that no exploit was available and that no exploitation in the wild had been reported.
HTTP/2 runs only where the Protocols directive turns it on, as the module documentation explains. The directive uses h2 for HTTP/2 over TLS and h2c for HTTP/2 over plain TCP. It can be set for the whole server or for a single virtual host, so admins should check the server-wide setting and every virtual host.
Standalone builds of the module, released on GitHub as mod_h2, are affected from version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.
Admins who run the Apache HTTP Server project's own releases should move to version 2.4.71, the fixed release named in its security advisory . That release also fixes a crash in mod_md, rated important, and a one-byte overwrite of stack memory in mod_vhost_alias, rated low.
The distributions in the table below ship their own builds of the server, with their own package version numbers. On Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9, for example, the fix ships as mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1.
Red Hat shipped fixes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 yesterday and rates the flaw Important on those releases rather than Critical. Their mod_http2 packages give each HTTP/2 stream its own memory allocator, which makes an attack much harder, according to the vendor's severity assessment . Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and earlier do not contain the vulnerable code.
The Debian rows come from Debian's security tracker , and the Amazon row from the Amazon Linux tracker . Ubuntu's CVE tracker had no page for the flaw when The Hacker News checked it today.
The Apache HTTP Server advisory offers no workaround. In its vulnerability analysis , Wiz advises admins who cannot update yet to remove h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive, leaving Protocols http/1.1.
The standalone mod_h2 project has published no fixed release so far. Its release list on GitHub ends at 2.0.42, the last affected version, and its repository has been read-only since it was archived on June 9. The Protocols change above also applies to servers that use those builds.
The flaw was reported on October 26 by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, a free scanning service for open-source projects that uses the company's AI models. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it last week.
An earlier HTTP/2 flaw , CVE-2026-23918, was fixed in version 2.4.67, released on May 4. Servers updated to that release, or to any later one up to 2.4.70, still run a version that the new flaw affects.

Chinese companies could unlock a further 15 per cent in equity valuation upside by stepping up share buy-backs and dividend payouts, as Beijing seeks to encourage listed firms to return more cash to investors, according to Goldman Sachs.
The US investment bank said in a report on Wednesday that an increase in corporate payout ratios and share repurchases, in line with policymakers’ efforts to improve shareholder returns, could lift valuations of the MSCI China Index by about 15 per cent from current levels through improved returns on equity and cash distributions to shareholders.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Tumbles as Investors Consider Future Without CEO Huang
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Tumbles as Investors Consider Future Without CEO Huang
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's board of directors is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang soon, according to two sources familiar with the matter, following allegations that Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believe was a Chinese asset.
The Trump administration is aware of the matter, the sources said.
The Wall Street Journal was first to report on the board's moves.
Nvidia's share price slid more than 8% in after-hours trading Wednesday after the Journal's report, extending a multi-day sell-off for one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies.
The company has faced days of turmoil following reports that American intelligence agencies believed Huang was the target of a Chinese spying plot.
Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993, and for years it was best known for designing graphics cards widely used for gaming. The company now designs the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.
The New York Times reported last week on allegations that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who previously led a Singapore-based firm called Megaspeed International that bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips and hardware. U.S. intelligence agencies have believed for months that Alice Huang — who is not related to Jensen Huang — was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, the newspaper reported.
In a message to Nvidia employees over the weekend, Jensen Huang wrote that he was "unfaithful to my wife" and apologized for hurting her and their children. He did not name the woman involved.
Nvidia's board said Sunday it had launched an independent investigation into allegations that the CEO "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." The board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."
Two law enforcement sources told CBS News the Justice Department is also investigating Megaspeed over potential violations of U.S. export restrictions on advanced AI chips. Some analysts have raised questions about whether the saga resulted in China — which is racing the U.S. for AI dominance — gaining access to Nvidia's technology through Megaspeed. The company has denied any involvement in illegal chip transfers.
China has denied all allegations, with Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun telling reporters on Monday that the "so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear."
Beyond the national security concerns, Nvidia is facing a securities lawsuit accusing the company of failing to disclose information to shareholders about Jensen Huang's relationship with the alleged spy.
Jensen Huang has a close relationship with the Trump administration. President Trump gave Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 computer chips to "approved customers" in China late last year, with the federal government taking a 25% cut of chip sales. The deal did not include Nvidia's more advanced Blackwell or Rubin systems.
The Nvidia CEO and other U.S. tech executives traveled to China with Mr. Trump earlier this year.
On Monday, Mr. Trump called Jensen Huang a "very high-quality person," saying during a White House briefing that "the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape." The president said he spoke to Jensen Huang to see how he was doing, and the executive "said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."
